decks.title: A World of Many Languages
decks.subtitle: How many languages do you hear in a single day?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: talk about languages and language skills with precise vocabulary
read about Mirandese and why minority languages are at risk
describe your own level in a language accurately and modestly
argue for or against a single global language

slides.title: Portugal's other official language
text: Most people think Portugal has one language. In fact, since 1999 the law has also recognised Mirandese, spoken in and around Miranda do Douro, close to the Spanish border.
For generations it survived at home and in the fields. Children were often told it was a rough way of speaking, so many families stopped passing it on.
Today it is an optional subject in local schools and appears on bilingual signs. Even so, linguists still class it as endangered, because most fluent speakers are older.

cards.text: Young people move to cities and use the majority language at work.

cards.heading: Revival
cards.text: Schools, music and online content can bring a language back.
cards.example: Welsh is now taught in all schools in Wales.

"It's raining cats and dogs" is an **idiom**.
She speaks **Portuguese** and **Mandarin**.

decks.title: The Tech World
decks.subtitle: Who is really in control: you or your phone?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: use current vocabulary about apps, data, privacy and AI
read a student's account of a month without a smartphone
weigh up the benefits and risks of AI tools at school

slides.title: My phone-free month
text: In October I swapped my smartphone for a basic phone that only calls and texts. The first week was awful. I kept reaching for my pocket, and I missed two plans because the group chat had moved without me.
By the third week, something changed. I was reading on the bus to school again and I fell asleep earlier. My screen time had been over five hours a day; now it was close to zero.
I'm back on my smartphone, but notifications are off and social apps live in a folder on the last screen. I'm not cured. I'm just more aware of who is choosing what I look at. (Inês, 16, Coimbra)

items.q: What two habits did she keep after the experiment?
items.a: She turned notifications off and hid social apps on the last screen.

items.q: What does she mean by "who is choosing what I look at"?
items.a: Apps and algorithms decide what she sees unless she is careful.

cards.heading: Fake content

cards.heading: Digital divide

decks.title: Media and Global News
decks.subtitle: Where do you get your news, and can you trust it?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: use key vocabulary about news, sources and misinformation
read how a misleading post spreads and how it is checked
understand the special grammar of news headlines
discuss how you get, judge and share information

left.heading: Misinformation
points: False or misleading content
Shared **without** the intention to deceive
Example: your aunt forwards a fake health tip
Fix: polite correction with a reliable link

right.heading: Disinformation
points: False content created **on purpose**
Aims to deceive, earn money or gain influence
Example: fake accounts spread lies before elections
Fix: report it, don't amplify it

slides.title: A photo that travelled too far
text: On a Friday evening, a photo of a flooded metro station appeared online with the caption "Lisbon, right now". Within an hour it had thousands of shares and angry comments about the city council.

The photo was real, but it had been taken in another country years earlier. A journalist found the original with a reverse image search and published a correction. By then, the false version had reached far more people than the fact-check would.
Researchers have shown that false stories often spread faster than true ones, because they are surprising and emotional. Checking takes time; sharing takes a second.

slides.instruction: Choose the best answer according to the text.

items.q: What was wrong with the photo?

items.a: It showed a different place and time.

items.q: How was the photo checked?

rows: A storm has hit the Algarve.

cards.heading: Who?
cards.text: Who published it? Is the author or outlet known and accountable?
cards.example: A named newspaper or a new anonymous account?

cards.heading: When?
cards.text: Old stories often return with a new date in the caption.
cards.example: Search the image to find its first appearance.

cards.heading: Evidence?
cards.text: Does it link to data, documents or other reliable outlets?
cards.example: "Experts say" with no names is a red flag.

cards.heading: Feeling?
cards.text: If a post makes you furious, slow down. That's often the goal.

slides.instruction: Complete each sentence with the correct word from the box.

points: **Misinformation** is accidental; **disinformation** is deliberate
Headlines: present for past, **to + verb** for future, no articles

decks.title: Youth in a Global Age
decks.subtitle: Closer to friends in Seoul than to your neighbours?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: talk about the opportunities and pressures young people face today
read about why young Portuguese adults leave home later
compare your generation with your grandparents' youth
talk about plans and ambitions with a range of structures

slides.title: Thirty and still at home
text: In Portugal, it is common to live with your parents until your late twenties, and sometimes longer. In Sweden or Finland, most young people have left by their early twenties. Laziness is not the reason.

Rents in Lisbon and Porto have risen much faster than salaries, and first jobs are often temporary. "I earn more than my mum did at my age, but a room in Arroios costs half my salary," says Tiago, 27, a nurse.
Some young people share flats with strangers; others emigrate. Many stay at home, save and wait. It works, but it delays independence, relationships and, for some, having children.

slides.instruction: Answer the questions about the text in your own words.

items.q: What is Tiago's point about his salary?

items.q: Name two consequences of staying at home longer.
items.a: It delays independence, relationships and sometimes having children.

News came from the radio and the café
Few travelled abroad, except to emigrate
Married and left home in their early twenties

right.heading: You at 16

News and opinions from everywhere, all day
Cheap flights, Erasmus+ and online friends abroad

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: understand where English is spoken and by whom
recognise key differences between British and American English

cards.heading: Inner circle
cards.text: English is the main first language of most people.
cards.example: UK, Ireland, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand

cards.heading: Outer circle
cards.text: English is official, used in schools, courts and the media.
cards.example: India, Nigeria, Singapore, Kenya, the Philippines

cards.heading: Expanding circle
cards.text: English is a foreign language for study, work and travel.

slides.title: Nobody's property
text: Picture a meeting in Brussels: a Portuguese engineer, a Polish manager and a Korean client. They all use English, and none of them is a native speaker. This is now the most common way English is used.
Speakers who learnt English as an additional language far outnumber native speakers. For them, the goal is not to sound like the King or a Hollywood star but to be understood.
Interestingly, native speakers are sometimes the hardest to follow in these meetings: they speak fast, use idioms and assume everyone shares their cultural references.

items.q: There are more non-native than native speakers of English.

items.fix: The main aim is to be understood.

items.q: Native speakers can be hard to understand in these meetings.
Idioms usually make international communication easier.
items.fix: Idioms can make native speakers harder to follow.

cards.heading: China: super-apps

slides.title: Who pays for the BBC?
text: The BBC is the UK's public broadcaster. Unlike most channels, it shows no adverts on its British TV and radio stations. Instead, households that watch live TV or use BBC iPlayer must pay an annual licence fee.

Supporters say this keeps the BBC independent from both advertisers and the government. Critics argue that it is unfair to charge everyone the same, whereas streaming services only charge people who choose them.
Portugal's RTP has a different model: it is funded mainly through a small fee on electricity bills, plus some advertising.

decks.title: Identity and Values
decks.subtitle: What really defines who you are?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: talk about identity, belonging and personal values
read a teenager's story of growing up between two cultures
use adjectives with the correct dependent prepositions
discuss the gap between our online and offline selves

cards.heading: Family and roots
cards.text: Language, food, religion and stories passed down at home.
cards.example: Sunday lunch at your grandparents' house.

cards.heading: Friends
cards.text: Our group sets what is cool, funny or embarrassing.
cards.example: The music you pretend to like.

cards.heading: Place
cards.text: Where we grow up colours how we speak and what we value.
cards.example: A Porto accent you never want to lose.

cards.heading: Online life

slides.title: Two homes, one me
text: I was born in Lyon to Portuguese parents. At home we spoke Portuguese, but my homework, my jokes and my dreams were in French. Every August we drove to my grandparents' village near Viseu, and there I was "the French girl".
When I was twelve, we moved back to Portugal for good. Suddenly my Portuguese sounded old-fashioned, and classmates laughed at my accent. I was proud of my roots but ashamed of not fitting in.
Now, at seventeen, I've stopped choosing. I dream in two languages, cook my mum's bacalhau and still miss French bakeries. Identity isn't a box. It's more like a playlist. (Mariana, 17)

slides.instruction: Answer the questions about Mariana's text.

items.q: Why was she called "the French girl" in the village?

items.q: What problem did she face when she moved to Portugal?
items.a: Her Portuguese sounded old-fashioned and classmates laughed at her accent.

items.q: Which two opposite feelings did she have at twelve?

items.q: What does she mean by "Identity isn't a box"?

points: Edited, filtered and carefully chosen

decks.title: Verb Tenses Review
decks.subtitle: Right time, right tense: no more guessing

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: choose confidently between simple and continuous forms
use the present perfect where Portuguese uses the present or past
tell a story with past simple, past continuous and past perfect
pick the right future form for plans, predictions and arrangements

slides.title: Present tenses
slides.note: Temporary situations take the continuous: I **live** in Braga, but this month I'**m living** in Porto.

slides.title: Stative verbs
slides.text: Verbs of **knowing**, **liking**, **owning** and **being** are not normally used in continuous forms. Some change meaning when they are.
examples: I **know** the answer. (not I'm knowing)
I **think** it's fair. (opinion) / I'**m thinking** about it. (process)
She **has** a car. (owns) / She'**s having** lunch. (eating)
This soup **tastes** great. / He'**s tasting** the soup.

slides.title: Simple or continuous?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct form.

left.heading: Past simple
points: Finished time, stated or understood
**yesterday**, **ago**, **last year**, **in 2019**
I **visited** London **last summer**.
**When** did you **start**? (question about time)

right.heading: Present perfect
points: Unfinished time or present relevance
**ever**, **never**, **yet**, **already**, **just**, **since**, **for**
I'**ve visited** London **twice**.
**How long** have you **studied** here?

slides.title: Portuguese trap: since and for
slides.text: Portuguese uses the present ("estou aqui desde...", "conheço-o há anos"). English needs the **present perfect** for something that started in the past and continues now.
examples: I'**ve been** here **since** 9 o'clock. (not I am here since)
I'**ve known** him **for** years. (not I know him for years)
She'**s been learning** the guitar **for** two months.

cards.heading: Past simple
cards.text: The main events, in order.
cards.example: I **opened** the door and **saw** him.

cards.heading: Past continuous
cards.text: Background, or an action interrupted by another.
cards.example: It **was raining** when the lights **went** out.

cards.heading: Past perfect
cards.text: An earlier past: something that happened before.
cards.example: The film **had** already **started**.

cards.heading: Used to / would
cards.text: Past habits that are no longer true.
cards.example: We **used to** spend August in Ericeira.

timetables, after when / as soon as

slides.title: Key takeaways
points: Stative verbs (**know**, **belong**, **prefer**) avoid continuous forms
Since / for + **present perfect**: I've lived here for years
Stories: past simple events, past continuous scenes, past perfect before
Arrangements: present continuous; no **will** after **when**

decks.title: Modal Verbs
decks.subtitle: He must have forgotten... or he can't have known?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: use modals for obligation, prohibition, advice and permission
tell the difference between mustn't and don't have to
make deductions about the present: must, might, can't
use perfect modals to speculate, criticise and regret the past

slides.title: Modals and their functions
slides.note: Modals take the bare infinitive (no **to**): she **can swim**, not she can to swim. **Ought to** and **have to** are exceptions.

left.heading: must / mustn't
points: **must**: obligation from the speaker
I **must** call Grandma, it's her birthday.
**mustn't**: it is forbidden, don't do it!
You **mustn't** cross on red.

right.heading: have to / don't have to
points: **have to**: rules from outside (school, law)
We **have to** be at school by 8.15.
**don't have to**: not necessary, it's your choice
You **don't have to** come, but it'd be nice.

slides.title: Rules and choices
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: You ___ smoke on school premises. It's illegal.
It's Saturday, so I ___ get up early.
You ___ see a doctor about that cough.
Last year we ___ wear a uniform.
You'd better ___ your bike or it'll get stolen.
Will you ___ come to the party on Friday?

cards.heading: must
cards.text: You're almost sure it's true, based on evidence.
cards.example: Her light's on. She **must be** home.

cards.heading: might / may / could
cards.text: It's possibly true; you're not sure.
cards.example: He **might be** stuck in traffic.

cards.heading: can't
cards.text: You're almost sure it's impossible.
cards.example: That **can't be** Rui. He's in Paris.

slides.title: Not mustn't!
slides.text: The opposite of **must** in deductions is **can't**, not mustn't. Mustn't is only for prohibition.
examples: She's wearing a coat. She **can't be** hot. (not mustn't be)
You **mustn't** touch that. (prohibition)

slides.title: Make a deduction
slides.instruction: Complete with must, might or can't + the verb in brackets.

items.q: He's been training all day. He ___ (be) exhausted.
That ___ (be) Marta's bag. Hers is red, this one's blue.

slides.title: Perfect modals: the past
rows: it was a good idea, but...
it was a bad idea, but...
it was possible, but didn't happen
slides.note: In speech, have is weak: "should've", "must've". Never write "should of".

slides.title: Comment on the past
slides.instruction: Rewrite each sentence using a perfect modal.

slides.title: needn't have vs didn't need to
slides.text: **Needn't have done**: you did it, but it wasn't necessary. **Didn't need to**: it wasn't necessary, and usually you didn't do it.
examples: I **needn't have cooked**: they'd already eaten. (I cooked)
I **didn't need to** cook: we ordered pizza. (I didn't cook)

slides.title: Which perfect modal?
slides.instruction: Choose the option that fits the situation.

slides.instruction: Match each situation to the most logical comment.

items.q: Nobody knows where the keys are.

slides.title: Key takeaways
points: **Mustn't** = forbidden; **don't have to** = not necessary
Deduction: **must** (sure yes), **might** (maybe), **can't** (sure no)
Past: modal + **have** + past participle: must **have gone**
**Should have** = criticism or regret; **could have** = lost chance

decks.title: Conditionals
decks.subtitle: If you had studied, would you be smiling now?

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: review zero, first, second and third conditionals
tell real possibilities from imaginary situations
build mixed conditionals that link past and present
use unless, as long as, provided that and in case

slides.title: The four main conditionals
rows: If I **had** a car, I'**d drive**.
if + past perfect, would have + pp
If I'**d known**, I'**d have come**.
slides.note: No **will** or **would** in the if-clause. Use a comma only when the if-clause comes first.

slides.title: Real or imaginary?
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.

items.q: If you ___ (mix) blue and yellow, you get green.
If Benfica ___ (win) on Sunday, they'll go top.
If I ___ (be) the minister, I'd lower rents.
We ___ (miss) the bus if we don't leave now.
If she ___ (speak) Japanese, she'd apply for that job.
What ___ you ___ (do) if you found a wallet?

left.heading: First: likely
points: You think it can really happen
If I **pass**, I'**ll celebrate**.
If it's sunny, we'**ll go** to Costa da Caparica.
Offers, warnings, threats

right.heading: Second: unlikely / unreal
points: Imaginary, improbable or impossible
If I **won** the Euromilhões, I'**d travel**.
If I **were** you, I'**d apologise**.
Advice, dreams, polite requests

slides.title: Choose carefully
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: If I ___ you, I'd talk to the teacher.
I'll lend you my notes if you ___ them back.
If humans ___ fly, cities would look different.
If you press that button, the alarm ___.

items.en: If I'**d set** an alarm, I **wouldn't have missed** the exam.
If they **hadn't scored** in the 90th minute, we'**d have won**.
She **would have come** if you'**d invited** her.
If Grandad **hadn't emigrated** to France, I **wouldn't have been** born there.
**Had** I **known**, I'd have told you. (formal inversion, no if)

slides.title: What if things had been different?
slides.instruction: Complete with the third conditional.

items.q: If you ___ (tell) me, I ___ (help) you.
We ___ (not / get) lost if we ___ (use) the GPS.
If it ___ (not / rain), the festival ___ (go) ahead.
She ___ (pass) if she ___ (revise) more.

cards.heading: Past cause, present result
cards.text: If + past perfect, would + verb (now).
cards.example: If I'**d studied** medicine, I'**d be** a doctor now.

cards.heading: Present cause, past result
cards.text: If + past simple (always true), would have + pp.
cards.example: If I **weren't** shy, I'**d have spoken** to her.

slides.title: Look for the time clues
slides.text: Ask two questions: **when** is the condition, and **when** is the result? Words like **now**, **today**, **still** or **yesterday** tell you which tense to use.
examples: If I hadn't stayed up late (yesterday), I wouldn't be tired **now**.
If she spoke English (in general), she'd have understood **the film**.

slides.title: Mix them up
slides.instruction: Rewrite each pair as one mixed conditional sentence.

items.q: I didn't sleep well. I'm exhausted now.
items.a: If I had slept well, I wouldn't be exhausted now.

items.q: He missed the flight. He isn't in London now.
items.a: If he hadn't missed the flight, he would be in London now.

items.q: I'm not good at maths. I didn't choose Science.
items.a: If I were good at maths, I would have chosen Science.

items.q: She doesn't like football. She didn't watch the final.
items.a: If she liked football, she would have watched the final.

items.q: We didn't buy tickets. We aren't at the concert.
items.a: If we had bought tickets, we would be at the concert.

slides.title: Beyond if
rows: You can go **as long as** you text me.
Take a jacket **in case** it gets cold.
slides.note: **In case** is not the same as **if**: we take the jacket now, whether it gets cold or not.

slides.title: Unless, as long as or in case?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct linker.

items.q: You won't get in ___ you show your ID.
Bring some cash ___ the card machine doesn't work.
You can borrow my bike ___ you bring it back today.
Write it down, ___ you'll forget.
I'll be there at eight ___ the train is late.

slides.title: Key takeaways
points: First = real future; second = imaginary now; third = imaginary past
No **will** / **would** in the if-clause; **If I were you**...
Mixed: **If I'd studied**, I'**d be**... / **If I were**, I'**d have**...
**Unless** = if not; **in case** = as a precaution

decks.title: The Passive Voice
decks.subtitle: It wasn't me: it was done!

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: form the passive in all the main tenses and with modals
decide when the passive is better than the active
use impersonal structures: it is said that, he is thought to
talk about services with have / get something done

slides.title: be + past participle
slides.note: Only the verb **be** changes tense. The main verb is always the **past participle**.

slides.title: Why use the passive?
slides.text: Use it when the action matters more than who did it, when the agent is unknown or obvious, and in formal writing, news and science. Add **by** + agent only if it is useful.
examples: My bike **was stolen** last night. (we don't know who)
The suspect **was arrested**. (obviously by the police)
Os Lusíadas **was written by** Camões. (useful information)

slides.title: From active to passive
slides.instruction: Rewrite in the passive. Include the agent only when it is useful.

items.q: Someone painted this mural in 2019.
The council is building a new bike lane.
items.a: A new bike lane is being built (by the council).

items.q: They have cancelled the match because of the storm.
items.a: The match has been cancelled because of the storm.

items.q: Millions of people watch this series.
items.a: This series is watched by millions of people.

items.q: You must hand in the project by Friday.
items.a: The project must be handed in by Friday.

cards.heading: Two objects
cards.text: The person usually becomes the subject.
cards.example: I **was given** a second chance.

cards.heading: -ing passive
cards.text: After verbs like enjoy, hate or avoid: being + pp.
cards.example: Nobody likes **being ignored**.

cards.heading: Infinitive passive
cards.text: After verbs like want, need or expect: to be + pp.
cards.example: She expects **to be chosen**.

cards.heading: get passive
cards.text: Informal, often for sudden or bad events.
cards.example: He **got fined** for speeding.

slides.title: Complete the passive
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct passive form of the verb in brackets.

items.q: The new hospital ___ (build) next year.
items.a: will be built / is going to be built

items.q: Sorry, the lift ___ (repair) at the moment.
By the time we arrived, all the pastéis ___ (eat).
I hate ___ (tell) what to do.
The winners ___ (give) a trip to the Azores last year.

slides.title: Impersonal passive
rows: **It is said that** the castle is haunted.
The castle **is said to be** haunted.
Subject + is believed to have + pp
He **is believed to have left** the country.
**It was reported that** two people were hurt.
slides.note: Common in news and essays with say, think, believe, know, report, expect and consider.

slides.title: News style
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences starting with the words given.

items.q: People say that the singer is very shy. (The singer...)
items.a: The singer is said to be very shy.

items.q: People believe that the thief escaped by boat. (It...)
items.a: It is believed that the thief escaped by boat.

items.q: Experts think the painting is a fake. (The painting...)
items.a: The painting is thought to be a fake.

items.q: People know that she earned millions. (She...)
items.a: She is known to have earned millions.

left.heading: Services we pay for
points: have + object + past participle
I **had my hair cut** yesterday.
We're **having the kitchen painted**.
**get** is more informal: I **got my phone fixed**.

right.heading: Bad experiences
points: Same structure, but not wanted!
She **had her bag stolen** in the metro.
He **had his account hacked**.
Compare: I cut my hair (myself) vs I **had** it **cut**.

slides.title: Somebody else did it
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of have something done.

items.q: My eyes are bad. I need to ___ (my eyes / test).
We ___ (the car / service) last week.
She's ___ (her nails / do) right now.

slides.title: Passive challenge
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

slides.title: Key takeaways
points: Passive = **be** (in any tense) + **past participle**
Use it when the action matters more than the agent
News style: **is said to be**, **is believed to have done**
Services: **have / get** + object + pp: I **had my hair cut**

decks.title: Reported Speech
decks.subtitle: She said what? Report it like a journalist

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: report statements with the right tense and time changes
report questions, commands and requests correctly
go beyond say and tell with precise reporting verbs
use each reporting verb with its correct pattern

slides.title: Tense changes (backshift)
rows: He said I **must / had to** go.
slides.note: **Say** something (to someone); **tell** someone something. Never "said me" or "told that" without a person.

slides.title: Time and place words
rows: the next day / the following day
the day before / the previous day
the following week / the week before
slides.note: These change only if the time or place is different when you report. Use common sense.

slides.title: When not to backshift
slides.text: If the reporting verb is in the present, or the fact is still true, you can keep the original tense.
examples: "I'm tired." He **says** he'**s** tired. (reporting now)
"The Earth goes round the Sun." She said the Earth **goes** round the Sun.
"I love Porto." He told me he **loves / loved** Porto. (still true)

slides.title: Report the statements
slides.instruction: Rewrite in reported speech, starting with the words given.

items.q: "I'm leaving tomorrow." (Rita said...)
items.a: Rita said (that) she was leaving the next day.

items.q: "We've lost the keys." (They told me...)
items.a: They told me (that) they had lost the keys.

items.q: "I'll text you later." (He said...)

items.q: "I saw this film last week." (She said...)

items.q: "You can sit here." (The guide told us...)

cards.heading: Wh- questions
cards.text: Keep the question word; use normal word order, no do/did.
cards.example: She asked where **I lived**.

cards.heading: Yes / no questions
cards.text: Use **if** or **whether** + normal word order.
cards.example: He asked **if I was** ready.

cards.heading: Commands
cards.text: tell + person + (not) to + verb.
cards.example: She told us **not to run**.

cards.heading: Requests
cards.text: ask + person + (not) to + verb.
cards.example: He asked me **to close** the door.

slides.instruction: Complete the reported sentences.

slides.title: Reporting verbs and their patterns
rows: accuse of, blame for, thank for
slides.note: **Suggest** never takes a person + to: "She suggested **going**" or "She suggested **that we go**".

slides.title: Which pattern?
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: He admitted ___ the window.
She persuaded me ___ the debate club.
They suggested ___ a taxi.
He apologised ___ late.
The coach warned us ___ underestimate them.

slides.instruction: Match each quote to the reporting verb that best describes it.

slides.instruction: Rewrite each sentence using the reporting verb in brackets.

items.a: She offered to help me with my CV.

slides.title: Key takeaways
points: Backshift: is → was, has done → had done, will → would
Reported questions: **if / whether** + normal word order
Commands and requests: **tell / ask** + person + **(not) to**
Learn the pattern: **refuse to**, **deny -ing**, **accuse of -ing**

decks.title: Relative Clauses
decks.subtitle: The friend who, the town where, the reason why

slides.title: In this lesson you will...
items: choose the right relative pronoun or adverb
tell defining from non-defining clauses and punctuate them
know when you can leave out the relative pronoun
use prepositions, whose, whom and which in more formal writing

slides.title: Relative pronouns and adverbs
rows: The girl **who** sits next to me is from Goa.
The bike **which** I bought is electric.
That's the boy **whose** dad is a pilot.
The café **where** we met has closed.
I remember the day **when** we won.

left.heading: Defining
points: Essential: tells us **which** one
No commas
**that** is possible
The students **who** passed got a certificate.

right.heading: Non-defining
points: Extra information: can be removed
Commas (or brackets) around it
**that** is NOT possible
My brother, **who** lives in Leeds, is a nurse.

slides.title: Leaving out the pronoun
slides.text: In defining clauses you can omit **who / which / that** when it is the **object** of the verb. If it is the subject, you must keep it.
examples: The film (**that**) we watched was dull. (object: can omit)
The film **that** won the prize was dull. (subject: keep it)
Never omit in non-defining clauses.

slides.instruction: Choose the correct relative pronoun or adverb.

story.title: Side B
story.subtitle: A school year, a box of old tapes and a voice nobody believed
story.blurb: In September, Mari Lobo finds a cassette hidden in her school's abandoned radio studio. On it, a girl's voice from 2003 says she has been blamed for something she didn't do, and that she knows who did. By June, Mari will have to decide how much the truth is worth, and who she is willing to lose for it.

characters.name: Mariana (Mari) Lobo
characters.desc: is fifteen and in 10.º B at the Calçada, a secondary school in Lisbon. She notices everything and says very little, except in Portuguese Sign Language, which she uses with her brother.

characters.name: Leonor Brás
characters.desc: has been Mari's best friend since they were six. She is loud, organised and determined to turn the school podcast into something serious. Her father reads the evening news on national television.

characters.name: Tobi Adeyemi
characters.desc: has just moved from London to Lisbon with his mother, an engineer. His parents are from Lagos. He is funny, curious about technology and still learning which Portuguese words are traps.

characters.name: Rui Quintela Câmara
characters.desc: is sixteen and repeating the year. He keeps to himself, and he seems to know far more about the old radio studio than he should.

characters.name: Duarte Lobo
characters.desc: is Mari's twelve-year-old brother. He has been deaf since birth, reads lips brilliantly and has strong opinions about everything.

characters.name: Henrique Salgado
characters.desc: runs a tiny second-hand bookshop in Mouraria. He used to teach English at the Calçada, until something happened in 2003 that he doesn't like to talk about.

chapters.title: The Room Behind the Stage
paragraphs: The new English teacher arrived ten minutes late, with wet hair, a bicycle helmet under one arm and a cardboard box of cassette tapes balanced on her hip.

"Sorry, sorry. Your hills have been trying to kill me since August," she said, and dropped the box on the desk. "I'm Fiona Doyle. I'm from Cork, which is in Ireland, which is not in England, so if anyone calls me English, I'll fail them. That's a joke. Mostly."

The twenty-six students of 10.º B laughed in the careful way people laugh on the first day of the year. Mariana Lobo, who had chosen the seat by the window because the window was the closest thing to an exit, laughed a second too late. She had spent the whole summer promising herself that secondary school would be different. She would speak in class. She would stop translating every sentence in her head three times before she said it out loud. So far, she had managed to sit down.

Beside her, Leonor Brás was already writing the teacher's name at the top of a fresh page, underlined twice. Leonor had been Mari's best friend since they were six, when she had taken charge of a sandpit in Graça and appointed Mari as her deputy. She had been taking charge of things ever since. This year it was the school podcast, which did not exist yet, but which Leonor had already named, designed a logo for and pitched to the head teacher in a very long email.

"This year," said Ms Doyle, "we're going to make a map. Not a map of places. A map of voices." She lifted a cassette out of the box and held it up like evidence in a courtroom. "Does anyone know what this is?"
"A fossil," said someone at the back.

"Close enough. I found a box of these in my flat when I moved in. When I was your age, I used to record the radio on these every Sunday night. Now everything lives on your phone, and nobody keeps anything." She put the cassette down. "Your project this term is to record people speaking the languages that actually live in this city. Your grandmother's village Portuguese. The Bengali in the shops on Rua do Benformoso. Kriolu on the 28 tram. English with a Lagos accent, a Glasgow accent, a Bangalore accent."
A boy in the second row turned round. He was new: tall, in a grey hoodie, with the expression of someone who had been stared at all morning and had decided to find it funny.
"Does English with a London accent count?" he asked.
"It counts more than mine, according to some people," said Ms Doyle. "What's your name?"

"Tobi. Tobi Adeyemi. I'm from London. Well, Peckham. My parents are from Lagos, my mum works for a tech company here now, and I've been in Lisbon for nineteen days." He held up his phone. "I've been using a translation app for everything. Last weekend we went to Porto and I asked for a bica, and the man in the café told me I was in the wrong city."

The class laughed properly this time. Tobi grinned and turned back, and Mari realised she had been doing the thing she always did with new people: guessing which of her languages she would need. Portuguese with her friends. English with films, books and the people inside them. And with her little brother Duarte, who was twelve and had been deaf since birth, Portuguese Sign Language, the language she had learnt before she could read, the one in which she was fastest and funniest and least afraid.
Nobody at school had ever asked her about that one.

"Before we start the project," Ms Doyle went on, "I need two volunteers. The school is finally clearing out the old student radio studio behind the auditorium. Rádio Eco. It closed years ago, and apparently there are boxes of tapes in there that nobody has touched since. The head would like someone to sort them before they're thrown away. Anyone?"
Leonor's hand was in the air before the sentence had ended. "We'll do it," she said. "Me and Mariana."
"I didn't..." Mari began.
"She's very organised," said Leonor.

That afternoon, the auditorium smelled of dust and floor polish. The stage curtains, which must have been red once, hung in heavy brownish folds. Behind them, past a stack of folding chairs and a cardboard tree from some forgotten Christmas play, there was a narrow door with a hand-painted sign that said, in Portuguese, ON AIR MEANS SILENCE.

Mr Abílio, the caretaker, unlocked it with a key from a ring that could have opened half of Lisbon. "Nobody has been in here since I started working here," he said. "And I started in 2004. Don't touch the wires."

The room was tiny. A mixing desk with half its sliders missing sat under a window that had been painted black. Two microphones leaned on their stands like tired birds. Posters were curling off the walls: a band Mari had never heard of, a football calendar from 2002, a timetable of presenters in coloured pens. Along one wall there were shelves, and on the shelves there were boxes.
"Right," said Leonor, pulling her hair into a knot. "You take the left, I take the right. We label everything. Date, content, condition."
"Since when do you know what condition a cassette is in?"
"Since I watched a video about it at lunch."

They worked for an hour. Most of the tapes were music copied from the radio, with titles like SUMMER MIX 2001 and DON'T TOUCH, IT'S ANA'S. There were interviews with teachers who had retired long ago and recordings of school concerts that sounded as if they had been made from inside a washing machine. Every box held the voices of people who had once been fifteen and loud and certain that what they were saying mattered.
Then Mari found the note.

It was not in a box. It was in her English textbook, which she had left open on a chair while she climbed up to reach the top shelf. A yellow sticky note had been pressed onto the page about phrasal verbs, right next to the words find out, and it had not been there at lunchtime. She was sure of that. On it, in block capitals, someone had written: SHELF 3. BEHIND THE BLUE BOX.

She looked at Leonor, who was sneezing over a crate of old newspapers. Then she looked at the door. It was half open. Through the gap she could see the dark stage, the cardboard tree and nothing else.
"Leo, did you put this in my book?"
"Put what?" Leonor did not even look up.

Mari counted the shelves. Shelf 3 was at eye level. There was a blue box labelled ENTREVISTAS 2002/03, and behind it, pushed against the wall as if someone had hidden it in a hurry, there was a single cassette in a cracked plastic case. The label was handwritten in faded blue ink: Para quem encontrar. M. 14/03/2003.
For whoever finds this.
"Leo," she said. "Come here."

Mr Abílio had left them an old cassette player, the kind with big square buttons, in case they needed to check what was on the tapes. Mari's hands were not completely steady when she pushed the cassette in. The machine whirred. For a few seconds there was only hiss, the soft roar of an empty room recorded a long time ago.
Then a girl spoke. She spoke in English, slowly and carefully, the way you speak a language you have learnt at school and are secretly proud of. In the background, something ticked like a clock.

"If you are listening to this, then somebody has finally opened the box. I don't know who you are. I don't know what year it is. But they are going to tell you that I did it, and I want you to know that I didn't. I know who did it. I just can't prove it yet. So I have left..."
The voice stopped. A heavy clunk came from somewhere on the tape, and then there was nothing but hiss.
"No, no, no." Mari pressed stop, then play. Hiss. Fast forward. Hiss.
"It must be broken," said Leonor quietly. For once, she did not sound as if she was in charge of anything.
"Or someone has recorded over the rest."
Behind them, the door creaked. Both girls turned round.

A boy was standing in the doorway, a boy Mari half recognised from the corridors: Rui Câmara, who was sixteen, who was repeating the year, and who, as far as anyone knew, had never volunteered for anything in his life. He was not looking at them. He was looking at the cassette player.
"You shouldn't be in here," he said. "Give me that tape."

chapters.title: A Map of Voices
paragraphs: Mari did not give him the tape.

Later, lying awake, she wondered why. She was not brave, usually. She was the kind of person who apologised to doors when she walked into them. But Rui had not said "give me that tape" like a bully. He had said it like someone asking for something that had been taken from him a long time ago, and that had made her close her hand around the cracked plastic case and slide it into her pocket.
"Why?" she asked.
"Because it isn't yours."
"It isn't yours either," said Leonor, who had recovered.

Rui looked at her for a long second. He had a thin white scar through one eyebrow and the tired eyes of someone who had not slept properly for a week. He opened his mouth, but at that moment Mr Abílio's keys jangled in the auditorium, and Rui stepped back into the dark. By the time the caretaker reached the door, he had disappeared.
"Friend of yours?" asked Mr Abílio.
"No," said both girls at once.
They argued about it all the way home on the 28 tram, squeezed between tourists with cameras. Leonor wanted to give the tape to the head teacher. "That's literally our job. Sort and report."
"Someone left that note for me," said Mari. "Not for the head. For me."
"You don't know that. It was in your book because your book was there."
"It was stuck next to find out, Leo."
Leonor rolled her eyes, but she did not argue any more, which was how Mari knew she had won.

October arrived with the smell of roast chestnuts on every corner and the first real rain. Ms Doyle put the class into groups for the language project, and by some miracle, or some plan Mari did not understand, Leonor, Mari and Tobi ended up together.
"I've never interviewed anyone," said Tobi, on the Saturday morning they met at Martim Moniz. "Unless you count my nan. And she interviews me."
"It's easy," said Leonor, who had prepared eleven questions and printed them. "You ask, they answer, we record. We should have finished by lunchtime."
They had not finished by lunchtime. They had not finished by four o'clock. Mouraria did not work like a list of questions.

In a narrow grocery shop that smelled of cardamom and wet cardboard, Mr Rahman stopped weighing lentils to explain that he spoke Bengali at home, Portuguese with his customers, Hindi from the films he had watched as a boy in Dhaka and English with "everybody else in the world". His daughter Nusrat, who was nine and wore football boots with a school uniform, corrected his Portuguese twice during the interview.
"In my house we speak three languages at dinner," Mr Rahman said, "and we argue in all of them."
On a bench by the church, Dona Celeste, who had come from Cape Verde in 1979, laughed at Leonor's first question until she had to wipe her eyes.

"Portuguese with a funny accent? No, filha. Kriolu is not broken Portuguese. It's my language. It has its own grammar, its own songs. My grandmother sang to me in it before I knew a single word of Portuguese." Then she sang a few lines, quietly, while the phone recorded, and nobody said anything for a while afterwards.
Leonor looked at her printed questions as if they had betrayed her. "That was a bit unfair of me," she said on the way down the steps. "The question, I mean. It was disrespectful."
"It was a bit uninformed," said Mari, and Leonor elbowed her.

Tobi was the surprise of the day. He talked to a delivery rider from Nepal called Bikash, who had learnt his English in Kathmandu, and the two of them spent twenty minutes discussing football, the Premier League and the price of rent in Lisbon, both of them switching between accents that were nothing alike.

"In London, people used to correct my mum's English," Tobi said afterwards, kicking a bottle top along the pavement. "In shops, at the doctor's. My mum. English is an official language in Nigeria. She's been speaking it her whole life. It's just not their English."
"Ms Doyle says nobody owns English," said Leonor.
"Ms Doyle says 'grand' when something is terrible," said Tobi. "I wouldn't trust her on everything."

Mari's brother had come with them, because their mum worked on Saturdays and their dad was in Germany on a contract until Christmas. Duarte had been bored for exactly ninety seconds, and then he had decided that the project was his. He pointed at things. He signed comments to Mari at a speed that made Tobi stare.
"What did he say?" Tobi asked.
"He said your microphone is pointing at your own nose."
Tobi adjusted it. Duarte signed again, grinning.
"And that you look like a nervous journalist."
"Tell him I am a nervous journalist." Tobi turned to Duarte directly, slowly, the way people always did. "How do you say 'thank you'?"

Duarte showed him. Tobi copied it, badly, and Duarte laughed so much that he had to sit on the kerb. Mari explained, while her brother recovered, that sign languages were not universal, that Portuguese Sign Language was mentioned in the Portuguese Constitution, and that British Sign Language and American Sign Language were completely different from each other.
"So if I'd learnt BSL in London," said Tobi, "it wouldn't have helped me here at all?"
"Not much. You'd have to start again."
"Story of my life," said Tobi.

It was Duarte who found the bookshop. It was squeezed between a barber's and a shop that sold phone cases, and it was so small that the sign above the door, LIVRARIA BABEL, was wider than the window. Inside, books in a dozen alphabets climbed to the ceiling. An old man with a white beard was reading behind the counter, and when Duarte waved at him, he put the book down and signed back: Good morning. It was slow and stiff, but it was right.
Duarte's whole face changed.

"I had a deaf student once," the old man explained to Mari, in Portuguese and then, noticing Tobi, in perfect English with a faint American accent. "A long time ago. She taught me more than I ever taught her. My name is Henrique Salgado. I used to teach at the Calçada, before you were born. Before your parents were sensible, probably."
On the bus home, Mari told Tobi about the tape. She had not planned to. It simply came out, between Martim Moniz and Graça, while Leonor was texting her mother and pretending not to listen.
"M.," said Tobi. "And she was speaking English. Why English?"
"So that nobody who found it by accident would understand?" Mari suggested. "In 2003, maybe most people at school didn't speak it very well."
"Or she wanted it to travel," said Leonor without looking up. "English goes further."
"She must have been a student," said Tobi. "She sounds about our age."
"She can't have been a teacher, anyway," said Mari. "And somebody might have recorded over the rest on purpose."
"Rui might have done it," said Leonor.
"Rui would have been about three in 2003."
"Then he must have known someone who was there."
Mari thought about the bookshop. Henrique Salgado had said he used to teach at the Calçada. Before you were born.

The following Saturday, she went back alone, with the cassette in her pocket. The bookshop was empty. Mr Salgado was mending the spine of an old Russian dictionary with glue and a paintbrush, and when she asked if he had a cassette player, he laughed.
"Look around you. I have everything that nobody wants any more."
He found one under the counter, dusty but working. Mari put the tape in and pressed play.
The girl's voice filled the tiny shop. If you are listening to this, then somebody has finally opened the box.

Mr Salgado's paintbrush stopped in mid-air. A drop of glue fell onto the dictionary and he did not notice. By the time the voice said I want you to know that I didn't, his face had gone the colour of old paper.
He reached out and pressed stop himself.
"Where did you find this?" he said, and his voice was not steady. "Who else has heard it?"
"Why? Do you know who she is?"
The old man walked to the door, turned the sign to CLOSED and locked it. Then he stood with his back to her for a long moment, looking out at the street.
"Her name is Marta Quintela," he said. "And the thing they said she did, they did it to me."

chapters.title: Lunchtime News
paragraphs: Mr Salgado made tea before he told her. He did it slowly, with his back to her, as if the tea were the most important thing in the world. Mari understood. Sometimes you need your hands to be busy while your mouth gets ready.

"In 2003, I had been teaching English at the Calçada for nineteen years," he said at last. "I was strict. I was boring, probably. I made people read Dickens. But I had never done anything wrong, and I thought that was enough."
He put a cup in front of her. It had a chip in the handle and a picture of the Eiffel Tower on it.

"The student radio played music at lunchtime. There were speakers in every corridor and in the canteen, so you couldn't escape it. On the fourteenth of March, in the middle of the lunchtime programme, there was a news bulletin. A fake one. A young man's voice, very serious, very professional. He said that a teacher at the school, Professor Henrique Salgado, had been selling the answers to the national exams. He said that the police were investigating. It lasted forty seconds." He sat down heavily. "By the time I had finished my soup, three hundred students had heard it."
"But it wasn't true."

"Of course it wasn't true. There was an inquiry. It took four months, and at the end of it they wrote a letter that said I was innocent. But by then a local newspaper had printed the story, parents had phoned the school, and people in the café on my street had stopped saying good morning. When you're accused of something on Monday, it's news. When you're cleared in July, nobody is listening." He shrugged, but his hands were tight around his cup. "I couldn't walk into a classroom again. I left the next year. I opened this shop. Books don't accuse anybody."
"And Marta?"

"Marta was the presenter that day. The bulletin was on a cassette in the pile of tapes she was playing, and she played it. She said she had never seen it before, that someone must have put it there. Nobody believed her. Her parents moved her to another school before Easter." He looked at the cassette on the counter. "I always thought she was telling the truth. She was a terrible liar. Once she told me her dog had eaten her homework, and she started laughing before she had finished the sentence."
"Then who did it?"
"If I knew that," said Mr Salgado, "I wouldn't be selling second-hand dictionaries."

Mari walked home through streets that suddenly looked different. A man was arguing on his phone outside a bar in a language she didn't recognise. Two girls were sharing headphones on a step. Somebody's radio was playing fado through an open window. Everyone was talking, all the time, in every language, and none of it was ever quite finished. She thought about forty seconds of somebody else's voice, and about how long a lie could live after it had been spoken.
She told Leonor and Tobi on Monday, in the corner of the library where the radiator was broken and nobody ever sat.
"That's unbelievable," said Tobi.

"It's actually very believable," said Leonor. "That's the problem." She was quiet for a moment, which was unusual. "My dad always says that a story only needs to sound true for about five minutes. After that, people don't check. They just remember."

Leonor's father was Paulo Brás, who presented the evening news on one of the national channels and was recognised in supermarkets. Leonor talked about him the way you talk about the weather: something you live with and occasionally complain about.
"We should have asked Mr Salgado for more names," said Tobi. "Who else worked on the radio. Who had a key."
"I couldn't. He was shaking."
"Then we look ourselves," said Leonor, and opened her laptop.

The school's old yearbooks were kept in a cupboard in the library, and nobody had borrowed the 2002/03 edition for a very long time. There was a photograph of the Rádio Eco team on page forty: eight teenagers squeezed around the mixing desk, pulling faces. Underneath, a list of first names only. Ana. Marta. Pedro. Paulo. Sofia. Nuno. Joana. Rui.
"Rui," said Leonor, pointing.
"A different Rui," said Mari. "This is 2003. That Rui must be about forty now."

The girl in the middle of the photo had short dark hair and was laughing at something outside the picture. Mari looked at her for a long time. She did not look like someone who was about to lose everything. Nobody ever does, she supposed.

November went by in the way the first term always did: too fast, then too slow, then too fast again. Tests came and went. Leonor launched the podcast with an episode about the school canteen's soup, which was more popular than anyone had expected. The language project was finished, edited and played to the class, and when Dona Celeste's song came on, Ms Doyle had to pretend she had something in her eye.
Rui Câmara did not speak to Mari once. But sometimes, in the corridor or in the queue for the canteen, she felt him watching her, and when she turned round he was always looking somewhere else.
On Christmas Eve, Tobi and his mum came to dinner. Mari's dad had flown back from Germany two days earlier, and the flat in Graça was hot, noisy and full of the smell of boiled cod and potatoes.
"So you eat cod on Christmas Eve," said Tobi, studying his plate as if it were a science experiment. "Boiled. With cabbage. On purpose."
"It's tradition," said Mari's grandmother, who had come down from Bragança and did not speak English but understood the tone perfectly.

"In my house we'd have jollof rice," Tobi told her, with Mari translating. "And my aunties would fight about whose jollof is the best. It's a whole thing between Nigerians and Ghanaians as well. A serious thing. Nobody wins."
Mari's grandmother nodded slowly, as if this were the first sensible thing she had heard from a foreigner in years.
Later, Tobi tried to explain in Portuguese that he was feeling a bit ill, and announced to the whole table that he was "constipado". Mari's mother patted his hand kindly. Tobi went pale.
"Did I just tell your family I can't go to the toilet?"
"No," said Mari, laughing so much she nearly knocked over the wine. "In Portuguese it means you've got a cold. It's a false friend."
"It's a terrible friend," said Tobi.
Duarte taught him three new signs that night, one of which Mari refused to translate.

On the last day of term, it was already dark when Mari left school. The gate was crowded with students in scarves and parents in cars with their hazard lights on. She was searching her bag for her bus pass when someone fell into step beside her.
"You played it to him," said Rui Câmara. "The tape. You played it to Salgado."
Mari stopped. "How do you know that?"

"Because he phoned my mother." Rui's breath made small clouds in the cold air. His hands were deep in his pockets and he would not look at her. "First time in twenty-two years. She hasn't stopped crying since."
"Your mother?"

He turned to her then, and in the orange light of the street lamp she saw it at last, the thing she should have noticed weeks ago: the same dark eyes, the same way of standing with one shoulder lower than the other, as the laughing girl on page forty of the yearbook.
"My name is Rui Quintela Câmara," he said. "Marta is my mum. And I'm the one who put that note in your book."
