chapters.title: Side B
paragraphs: Mari spent the whole Christmas holiday thinking about what Rui had said, and the first week of January avoiding him.
It did not work. On the second Monday of term, he sat down opposite her in the library, in the corner with the broken radiator, as if he had been invited.
"You haven't told anyone," he said. It was not a question.
"Only Leonor and Tobi."
"So, everyone."
"They're not everyone." Mari closed her book. "Why me? Why did you put the note in my book and not just go in there yourself?"

Rui looked at the table. "Because I'm not allowed in the auditorium. I broke a window there last year. Long story, stupid story." He picked at the edge of the table with his thumbnail. "And because I'd seen you. In here, reading books in English that weren't for school. Signing to your brother at the bus stop. You notice things. I thought, if anyone finds it and actually listens, it'll be her."
It was the strangest compliment Mari had ever received, and she did not know what to do with it, so she asked the question that had been keeping her awake.
"How did you know the tape was there?"

"I didn't. Not for sure." He spoke quickly now, as if he had been carrying the words around for a long time. "My mum never talks about that school. Never. When I was little, I thought she had just been a bad student. Then last year I found an old newspaper in a drawer, with the story about Salgado, and her name underlined. And one night I heard her on the phone to her sister. She said, 'If I had kept the tape, none of this would still be hurting.' Then she said, 'It's probably still behind the blue box, rotting.'" He shrugged. "So I looked for a blue box."
"Does she know what you've done?"
"She does now. Salgado made sure of that." He finally looked up. "She won't talk to me about it. She says if I keep digging, I'll only get hurt. She says some things are better left buried."
"Do you believe that?"
"If I believed that," said Rui, "I wouldn't be sitting here."

The tape was the problem. It had been played so many times now that Mari was afraid it would snap, and the clunk in the middle of Marta's message still bothered her. It had not sounded like the end of a recording. It had sounded like something falling.
It was Tobi who suggested having it digitised.

"My mum's company has a sound lab," he said at lunch, pushing rice around his plate. "They test microphones for cars. Voice commands, that kind of thing. If we had the tape copied properly, with good equipment, we could clean the sound up and actually look at it."
"Look at it?" said Leonor.
"Sound is just data. If you turn it into a picture, you can see things you'd never hear." He was already taking his phone out. "I'll ask her tonight. If she says yes, we can have it done this week."

His mother said yes, on one condition: that nobody touched anything without asking. On Thursday afternoon, the four of them, Mari, Leonor, Tobi and, to Leonor's visible annoyance, Rui, stood in a white room on the fourth floor of an office building near the river, watching an engineer called Sandra feed Marta's cassette into a machine that looked as if it belonged in a spaceship.
"It's in better shape than I expected," Sandra said. "Old tapes like this were made to last, if they were kept dry. Give me ten minutes."

Tobi's mum had left them to it. Through the glass wall they could see her on a video call, laughing and switching between English and Yoruba every few sentences, while somebody's grandmother in Lagos waved at the camera.
"That's my aunt," said Tobi. "She sends voice notes. Long ones. Seven, eight minutes. My whole family runs on voice notes. Nobody in Nigeria wants to type if they can talk."
"My grandmother still phones the landline," said Mari. "Every Sunday at eight. If you don't answer, she assumes you're dead."
"And Duarte?"
"Video calls. With his friends from his old school, all signing at once. It's like watching a football match with no ball."
"My mum doesn't have a phone at all," said Rui. Everyone turned to look at him. "Well, she has one. A really old one. No internet. She says she's had enough of things that stay on record forever."
Nobody knew what to say to that.

The file came up on Sandra's screen as a long blue landscape of peaks and valleys. She showed them how the spectrogram worked: time from left to right, pitch from bottom to top, loudness as colour. Marta's voice was a band of bright shapes in the middle. The hiss was a grey fog over everything.
"There's your clunk," said Sandra, pointing. "Something hit the microphone. A hand, maybe, or the door. Then she stopped recording. It wasn't recorded over. It just ends."
"So she was interrupted," said Mari.
"Or she panicked," said Leonor.
Sandra had stopped listening to them. She had leaned closer to the screen and was frowning at the fog under Marta's voice.
"That's odd," she said. "There's something else in here. Underneath."

She turned up the volume and isolated the frequencies. Through the speakers, below the hiss, came something none of them had heard before: a faint, warbling sound, like a voice under water, rising when it should fall and falling when it should rise.
"Is that a ghost?" said Tobi, only half joking.

"It's the other side," said Sandra. "Side B. On a cassette, both sides are recorded on the same strip of tape, side by side, running in opposite directions. If you turned this one over, you'd hear nothing, because somebody recorded silence over side B. But old machines never erased everything. There's a ghost of the original recording left, and some of it has leaked across to this side. That's why it's backwards." She was already clicking. "If I reverse it and clean it up, we'll find out what it is."

It took her twenty minutes. Nobody spoke. Rui stood by the window with his arms crossed so tightly that his knuckles were white, and Mari realised that she had never seen anyone want something so much and be so afraid of getting it.
Then Sandra pressed play.
A boy's voice, young but trying to sound older, came out of the speakers. The words were blurred, broken up by the hiss, but some of them were perfectly clear.
"Lunchtime news... a teacher at this school... Henrique Salgado... selling the answers to the national exams..."
A pause. Then the same voice, normal now, relaxed, laughing at someone off the microphone.
"No, it's fine. She never checks the tapes. Quintela just plays whatever's on the pile. Nobody will ever know it was me."
The recording ended with a click.

For a long moment, the only sound in the white room was the air conditioning. Then Rui turned away from the window and walked out without a word, and they heard the door of the stairwell bang shut behind him.
"If someone had found this in 2003," said Leonor slowly, "everything would have been different."
"If Marta had had a spectrogram in 2003," said Tobi, "she wouldn't have needed anyone."
Mari said nothing. She was thinking about the voice. She felt as if she had heard it before, somewhere, a long time ago, through a wall or in a dream.
Sandra copied the files onto a memory stick and Tobi put them in a shared folder, so that none of them could lose anything. They walked to the metro in silence. Rui did not answer his phone.
That night, at a quarter to midnight, Mari's phone buzzed on her pillow. A new follower. The account had no photo, no posts and no bio. Only a name: @radioeco2003.
A second later, a message arrived.
You found Side B. Be careful who you play it to.

chapters.title: Taken Down
paragraphs: Mari did not sleep. She lay in the dark with her phone face down on her chest, reading the message again every few minutes as if the words might rearrange themselves into something less frightening.
Be careful who you play it to.

Only four people had heard Side B. Five, if you counted Sandra, and Mari did not believe for one second that a sound engineer in her forties had created an anonymous account at midnight to threaten teenagers. That left Leonor, Tobi and Rui. And herself.
At two in the morning, she wrote back: Who are you?
There was no answer.

For a week, nothing happened. The account sat on her phone like a stone in a shoe. She checked it before breakfast, between lessons, in the queue for the canteen. Nothing. Rui came back to school on the Monday as if he had never walked out of the sound lab, and when Mari asked him about the account, he looked at her with such blank surprise that she felt stupid for asking.
"If I wanted to talk to you," he said, "I'd talk to you."
Leonor laughed when Mari showed her. "It's a bot. Or someone from 12.º who heard us talking in the library. Ignore it."
Tobi did not laugh. "Whoever it is knows about Side B," he said. "That's not a bot."
Then, on the Thursday before Carnival, the account woke up.

The first post appeared at twenty past ten, during break. It was a black square with white letters: IN 2003, A GIRL WAS BLAMED FOR A LIE. SHE SAID SHE DIDN'T DO IT. NOBODY LISTENED. Underneath, there was a forty-second clip: Marta's voice, cleaned up by Sandra's software, clearer than Mari had ever heard it. If you are listening to this, then somebody has finally opened the box.
By lunchtime it had been shared by half the school. By the end of the day, it had been viewed eleven thousand times.

Everybody had a theory. The voice was an actress. The voice was AI. The whole thing was a marketing campaign for a series. A girl in 11.º claimed that her aunt had been at the Calçada in 2003 and remembered "something about a teacher and a scandal". Somebody found the old newspaper article and posted a photo of it. By Friday, Henrique Salgado's name was being typed into search engines all over Lisbon for the first time in more than twenty years.
Mari watched it happen with a cold feeling in her stomach. It was like watching a fire you had accidentally started spread across a field.
On Friday afternoon, she was called to the head teacher's office.

Dr Teresa Monteiro was a small, precise woman who wore reading glasses on a chain and was rumoured never to have smiled before eleven in the morning. She did not offer Mari a seat. Ms Doyle was already there, standing by the window with her arms folded.
"You and Leonor Brás were asked to sort the radio archive," said Dr Monteiro. "Were you not?"
"Yes."

"And at some point during that work, a cassette was removed from the school without permission. A cassette that is now, apparently, on the internet." She turned her laptop round. The black square filled the screen. "Do you know who is responsible for this account?"
"No."

"Mariana, I'll be honest with you. This has been brought to my attention by three parents, a journalist and the Ministry. The posts have been reported, and I've had the account taken down twice this week. It keeps coming back. Your locker is going to be checked this afternoon, and if I find that you have been involved..."
"She has said she doesn't know," said Ms Doyle quietly. "I believe her."
"Then she won't mind the locker being checked."

Mari's locker was opened by Mr Abílio, who looked deeply embarrassed about it. Nothing was found apart from a PE kit that needed washing and three pens that didn't work. Mari was allowed to go, but at the door Dr Monteiro said something that followed her all the way home.
"If you had brought that tape to me in September, Mariana, we wouldn't be in this situation now."

It was true, and that was the worst part. If she hadn't opened the box, she wouldn't be in this mess. If she hadn't played the tape to Mr Salgado, Marta wouldn't be crying again after twenty-two years. If, if, if. Her whole life suddenly seemed to be made of sentences that started with if.

"You can't think like that," said Tobi on Saturday, at the Carnival parade in Torres Vedras, where Leonor had dragged them both because her family went every year. He was dressed as a cassette tape, in a costume he had had made by a woman in his building who usually repaired wedding dresses. "If you think like that, you'll never do anything."
"I don't want to do anything. I want to go back to September."

"In London, my school locked our phones in pouches every morning," said Tobi, adjusting one of his cardboard spools. "You got them back at half three. It was annoying, but nothing like this ever went round in a single morning. Here everyone's in fourteen group chats by the age of ten."
"So it's our fault for having phones?"

"I'm saying a rumour moves at the speed of whatever it's riding on. In 2003 it was a radio. Now it's this." He waved at the crowd, where at least a hundred people were filming the same float of men dressed as giant babies. "And you can't switch this off."

Leonor came back from the food stall with three farturas and an expression Mari couldn't read. She had been strange for days. Quiet, then too loud. Checking her phone and then putting it away fast, screen down. When the clip went viral, she had said almost nothing, which for Leonor was like a fire alarm going off.
"Are you okay?" Mari asked.

"Fine. Just my dad. He's being weird." Leonor handed out the farturas. "Someone at his channel wants to do a story about the clip. A whole report. He told them to drop it. He said it was a waste of time, that it was just kids playing with old tapes." She bit into her fartura. "He never tells anyone to drop a story. Never. He'd report on a cat stuck in a tree if it got viewers."
Tobi met Mari's eyes over Leonor's head, and neither of them said anything.
On Monday morning, the account was back for the third time, with a new name, @radioeco2003_, and a new post.

It went up at twenty past ten, during break, just like before. Mari was standing in the corridor outside the chemistry lab when her phone buzzed, and then everyone's phone buzzed, all along the corridor, like a swarm of insects waking up.
It was another clip. But this time it was not Marta's voice.

It was the boy. The young voice, trying to sound older, cleaned and reversed and perfectly clear. No, it's fine. She never checks the tapes. Quintela just plays whatever's on the pile. Nobody will ever know it was me.
Mari's hands went cold.
Side B had never been shared with anyone. It was in one place only: a folder that four people had access to. The account had not found it, guessed it or stolen it from Sandra's lab.
It had been posted by one of them.

chapters.title: Faces Without Sound
paragraphs: Mari found Rui behind the sports hall, where the smokers went and the teachers pretended not to know. He was sitting on an upturned crate with his phone in his hand, watching the numbers under the new post go up.
She did not say hello. She held out her own phone, with the clip on the screen.
"Was it you?"

He did not even try to deny it. That was the thing she would remember later: he didn't lie, not for a second. He just looked up at her, and his face was tired and defiant and somehow relieved, as if he had been waiting for someone to ask.
"Yes."
"All of it? From the start? The message at midnight?"
"All of it."
"You copied Side B from Tobi's folder."
"He gave me the link. I didn't break into anything."

Mari sat down on the wall opposite him because her legs had decided they didn't want to hold her any more. "Do you know what happened to me on Friday? I was called into Monteiro's office. They searched my locker. She thinks I did it."

"I know. I'm sorry." And he did sound sorry, which made it worse. "I didn't think they'd go after you. I thought they'd go after the account. I thought..." He stopped and started again. "Twenty-two years, Mari. Twenty-two years my mum has been the girl who did it. She didn't go to university. She didn't do anything she wanted to do. She works nights in a hotel and she doesn't have the internet because she's scared of her own name. And the guy who actually did it is out there somewhere, laughing. You heard him laughing."
"So you decided to make a mess on the internet."
"If somebody had made a mess in 2003, my mum wouldn't be like this now." He stood up. "I'm not going to say sorry for that part."

It was Leonor who found them. She had obviously worked it out at the same time as Mari, because she came round the corner of the sports hall already shouting, and for the next five minutes Mari didn't need to say anything at all. Leonor said it for her. She said that Rui had got Mari into trouble. She said that he was a coward hiding behind a username. She said that people like him were the reason the internet was a sewer. Then she said something about his mother that made Rui go very white and very quiet, and Mari had to step between them.
"Stop it. Both of you."
They stopped. Leonor was breathing hard. She looked, Mari thought, much angrier than the situation explained, angry the way you get when you are really frightened of something else.

"Take the clips down," Mari said to Rui. "Please. Just for now. Give us time to find out who the boy is. If we know his name, we won't need the internet. We can go to Monteiro, to the newspapers, to whoever. Properly."
Rui looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded once, took out his phone, and the account disappeared while they watched.
Finding out who the boy was turned out to be harder than any of them had imagined.

They went back to the yearbook. They went back to the list of names on page forty. They looked for every Pedro, Paulo and Nuno who had been at the Calçada in 2003, and found a dentist in Coimbra, a chef in Toronto and a man who sold solar panels in the Algarve. None of them sounded right. Tobi tried a voice comparison app, which compared Side B with old interviews on the radio shelves and gave answers so random that he deleted it in disgust.
"It's useless," he said. "If it were that easy, the police would never need witnesses."
It was Mr Abílio, of all people, who gave them the next clue. He came into the library on a wet afternoon in early March, carrying a plastic bag.
"You girls catalogued these in September," he said, putting three black video cassettes on the table. "VHS. The head wants them thrown out with the rest. I thought you might want a look first."
One of the labels said FESTA DA PRIMAVERA 14/03/2003.
The fourteenth of March. The day of the fake bulletin.

They had the tape converted at a little shop near Rossio, run by a man who seemed thrilled that anyone still wanted VHS. When he gave them the memory stick, he apologised. "The picture's fine, more or less," he said. "But the sound's gone completely. Damp got into it. You'll only have the images."

They watched it that evening at Mari's flat, all of them on the sofa: Mari, Tobi and Rui, with Duarte sitting cross-legged on the floor because he refused to miss anything. Leonor had said she couldn't come. Podcast meeting, she had texted. Mari had not believed her.

The video was long and wobbly and mostly boring. A band in the playground, playing to six people and a dog. Teachers pretending to dance. A younger, darker-haired Mr Salgado, standing at the edge of the crowd with a paper cup in his hand, smiling at something a student had said. Rui made a small noise when he saw him, and nobody looked at anyone. Twenty minutes later, the camera turned to a group of girls by the canteen door, and one of them, short dark hair, laughing, was his mother. Mari heard him hold his breath until she had gone out of the frame. Then the camera moved inside, along the corridor towards the auditorium, and Rui leaned forward.

A door at the end of the corridor opened. The narrow door behind the stage. A tall boy came out of it, laughing, and slid a cassette into the pocket of his jacket. Another boy was waiting for him. The tall one said something, turned to look over his shoulder at the studio door and said something else.
There was no sound. Just two mouths moving in silence.

Duarte sat up straight. He grabbed the remote control, rewound and played it again, his eyes fixed on the screen. Then he played it a third time, slower. Mari knew that look. Duarte had been reading lips since before he could tie his shoelaces. He could read a referee's swearing from the top of a stadium.
He turned to her and signed, very clearly.
"What's he saying?" said Rui. "Mari. What's he saying?"

Mari watched her brother's hands and translated, her own voice sounding strange to her. "He says the boy says: 'Done. It's on her pile.' And then the other one asks something, and the tall boy says: 'Relax. She'll take the blame, not me.'"
Nobody moved.
On the screen, as if he had heard them, the tall boy turned round. He saw the camera and grinned, a big confident grin, and pointed at the lens like a presenter introducing the next item on the news.
Mari pressed pause.

The face was younger, thinner, with too much gel in its hair. But she knew it. She had seen it on television a thousand times, reading the evening news in a dark suit. She had seen it at the head of a kitchen table in Graça, telling stories while Leonor rolled her eyes. She had seen it at her own seventh birthday party, holding the camera.

She could hear the blood in her ears. Beside her, Tobi was frowning at the screen. On the floor, Duarte had gone completely still. Rui was looking from the screen to her face and back again, trying to understand.
"Who is it?" he said. "Mari, who is that?"
Mari could not take her eyes off the frozen grin.
It was Paulo Brás. It was Leonor's father.

chapters.title: What Friends Are For
paragraphs: Duarte was the first to move. He looked up at his sister and signed, small and fast, close to his chest, the way they used to whisper in church when they were little: That's Leonor's dad.
Mari signed back without thinking: Not a word. Not to anyone.
Rui could not read sign language, but he could read faces, and he had seen enough. "You know him," he said.
"I thought I did. I don't." It was the first real lie Mari had told in months, and it came out badly. "It's an old video. Everyone looks the same with that much gel."
Rui stared at her. Then he picked up his jacket and left without saying goodbye, and Mari understood that he did not believe a word of it, and that he would not forgive her for it either.
She told Tobi the truth an hour later, on the phone, sitting on the floor of the bathroom with the tap running so that her mother wouldn't hear.
"I didn't know who he was," Tobi said, when she had finished. "I've only been here eight months. I don't watch Portuguese news. I thought he was just some guy."
"He's not just some guy. He's the guy who reads the news to the whole country every night. And he's Leo's dad."
"So what are you going to do?"
"I don't know. That's why I'm phoning you."
Tobi was quiet for a long time. "My grandad used to say that a secret is a debt," he said finally. "Somebody always pays for it. The question is just who."

The Easter holidays began two days later. Mari had never been so grateful for a holiday in her life, and never so miserable during one. She stayed in. She ignored three messages from Leonor and answered the fourth with a single word. She read the same page of her book eleven times.

On Easter Sunday, her grandmother phoned the landline at eight o'clock exactly and asked why she sounded like a wet cat. Mari said she was tired. Her grandmother, who had raised four children and believed none of them, said that tiredness was something you got from work, and that what Mari had was something else. Then she told her about a neighbour in Bragança who had kept a secret from her sister for thirty years, although the secret, in the end, had turned out to be about a goat. Mari laughed for the first time in a week. It did not help for long.

On the Wednesday, she went to Livraria Babel. Mr Salgado was sitting in the doorway in the sun, which was something she had never seen him do. He listened to everything without interrupting, and when she had finished, he did not seem surprised.

"Paulo Brás," he said. "Of course. I failed him in his final English test. I caught him copying from a boy who sat next to him. He told me I would regret it. I thought he was being dramatic. Teenagers always are." He looked at the people passing in the street. "He was a very talented boy, you know. Charming. The kind of student that every teacher likes, until they don't."
"What should I do?"

"I can't tell you that. I can only tell you what I've learnt, which is that the truth arrives late, but it does arrive." He turned to look at her. "However, it isn't your truth to throw at your friend like a stone. If you do that, you'll lose her, whether you're right or not."

When school started again, everything had moved on without her. A boy in 12.º had reported Rui to the head, and Rui had been suspended for five days while the school decided what to do with him. Dr Monteiro had told his mother that the account had been a form of cyberbullying, and she had warned her that if it happened again, he would be expelled. Rui had refused to apologise. He had also refused to say how he had got the clips, which, Tobi pointed out, meant that he was protecting them.
"Or protecting himself," said Mari.
"He's not stupid. If he told them about the folder, they'd know you had the tape all along."

Leonor, meanwhile, was busier than ever. Her podcast, which had started with soup, had been chosen for an online youth media exchange that Ms Doyle had organised with schools in Cork, Accra and Pune. Each school had to produce one episode on a story that mattered to young people in their community, and the four episodes would be streamed live at the end of the year, to an audience of students on three continents. The school in Accra was making an episode about young people's music on social media. The one in Pune was investigating how fake news travels through family group chats. The students in Cork had chosen emigration, a subject which, Ms Doyle said, every family in Ireland had an opinion about.

"And we're doing Rádio Eco," Leonor announced in the library, with the expression she used to have when she won at board games. "It's the biggest story this school has had in twenty years, and we're the only ones who've actually heard the tapes. My dad says it's a terrible idea." She laughed. "Which, obviously, means it's a great one."
Mari looked at her best friend, who had been her best friend since a sandpit in Graça, who knew her better than anyone except Duarte, and found that she could not say a single word.
That week, Ms Doyle held a debate in English class. The motion, which she wrote on the board in large letters, was: A good friend always tells the truth.

Most of the class agreed. Inês said that friends who lied to protect you were treating you like a child. Gonçalo argued that the truth was overrated, because if everyone said what they really thought, nobody would have any friends at all. Somebody at the back claimed that her grandmother lied about her age to everyone, including the doctor, and lived very happily. Tobi said that it depended on whose truth it was, and who would get hurt by it, and why you wanted to tell it. Ms Doyle said that was the most sensible thing she had heard all year and that she was going to steal it.

Leonor spoke last, as she always did. "The truth is the truth," she said. "If someone you love has done something wrong, you have to know. Otherwise you're living in a lie, and you don't even know you're in it. I would rather be hurt than be lied to."
She was looking at the board when she said it. She was not looking at Mari. But Mari felt the words land in her chest like something heavy and cold.

That Friday, Leonor's laptop died in the middle of editing. She came round to Mari's flat with a hard drive and a packet of biscuits, the way she had done a hundred times before, and asked to borrow Mari's computer.
"Just for an hour. I need to finish the trailer for the exchange. Ms Doyle wants it on Monday."

"Sure," said Mari, because she could not think of a single reason to say no that would not need explaining. She went to make tea. She stayed in the kitchen longer than she needed to, listening to the kettle and to Duarte arguing with a video game in the next room.
When she came back with the cups, the room was very quiet.

Leonor was sitting in front of the laptop. She had not opened her editing software. On the screen, frozen in the middle of a grin, a seventeen-year-old boy with too much gel in his hair was pointing at the camera.
Leonor did not turn round. When she spoke, her voice was perfectly calm, and that was the most frightening thing of all.
"How long have you known?"

chapters.title: Off the Record
paragraphs: "Since March," said Mari.

She could have said more. She could have explained about Duarte and the lip-reading, about Mr Salgado and the stone, about the hundred times she had nearly picked up the phone. But Leonor had already stood up. She unplugged her hard drive, put it in her bag, and walked past Mari to the door without touching her, carefully, the way you walk past a dog you don't trust.
"You let me plan a whole episode," she said from the hallway. "You sat there in the library and let me talk about it."
The front door closed. It did not even slam. Somehow that was worse.

For two weeks, Leonor Brás did not speak to her. She moved seats in English. She sat with girls from 10.º A at lunch, laughing a bit too loudly. When they passed in the corridor, she looked through Mari as if she were a window, and Mari, who had spent nine years being the quiet one in a friendship with the loud one, discovered that silence is much louder when it comes from the other person.
Then, at ten past two on a Thursday morning, her phone lit up with a voice note. Eleven minutes long. Mari listened to it under the duvet, with one earphone, holding her breath.

Leonor's voice was hoarse, as if she had been crying, or shouting, or both. She said that she had shown her father the frame from the video. She said that at first he had laughed and asked where she had got it. Then he had stopped laughing. He had told her that the video proved nothing, that it was a silent film of a teenager coming out of a room, and that anybody could put words into a silent mouth. He had asked her who else had seen it. He had warned her that if the story came out, it would destroy everything: his job, the family, her mother's peace. He had begged her to cancel the episode.

"And here's the thing, Mari," said Leonor's voice in the dark, very quietly. "He never said he didn't do it. Not once. He said I couldn't prove it. He said nobody could prove it. That's not the same, is it? That's not the same at all."
There was a long pause on the recording, full of breathing.
"I'm still angry with you. I want you to know that. But I think I understand why you didn't tell me. I wouldn't have told me either."
Mari played it three times. Then she wrote back: I'm here. Whenever.
The answer came at once: I know. Go to sleep.

The story would not stay quiet, either. At the beginning of May, a national newspaper ran a short article about "a cyberbullying case at a Lisbon secondary school", in which an anonymous account had used "old recordings of uncertain origin" to accuse "a former student, now a public figure". There were no names. There didn't need to be. The article quoted a source close to the school who said the recordings could easily have been manipulated, "especially now, when anyone with a laptop can fake a voice".

Two days later, Dr Monteiro received a letter from a law firm whose offices took up three floors of a glass building on Avenida da Liberdade. The letter said that its client, whose name it did not give, was concerned that "private material" was being kept by students, and it requested that all copies should be handed over to the school and destroyed.
Rui's disciplinary hearing was set for the second week of June.

It was Rui who arranged the meeting with his mother. He did not explain how he had persuaded her, and Mari did not ask. They met at seven o'clock on a Saturday morning in a café in Alfama, at the end of Marta's night shift. She arrived in the uniform of the hotel where she worked, a grey jacket with a name badge she had forgotten to take off. Close up, she looked older than forty and younger than her voice on the tape, which was a strange combination. She ordered a galão and did not touch it.
"So you're the girl who opened the box," she said, in English, smiling slightly. "My son says you notice things."
"Your son says a lot of things about me that aren't true."
"Not that one, I think."

She told the story slowly, in a mixture of English and Portuguese, stopping sometimes to look out of the window at the river. She told them that she had suspected Paulo from the start. He was the boy who had threatened Salgado, the boy who had a key to the studio, the boy who always laughed a second before everybody else. She said she had gone to the head the day after the bulletin and told him so, and that the head had told her not to make accusations she could not support. "Paulo was everyone's favourite," she said. "His father was on the parents' committee. I was the girl from the flats behind the market. You can guess whose word was worth more."

The week before her parents took her out of the Calçada, she had gone back to the studio one last time. She had picked up a blank tape from the pile on the shelf, the pile everyone used, and she had started to record a message for nobody: for the future, for whoever would come one day and listen properly.
"Then the door opened," said Marta, "and it was him."
Nobody at the table moved.

"He just stood there and looked at me. He didn't say anything. He didn't need to. I hit the microphone, I stopped the tape, and I waited for him to go. When he had gone, I hid it behind the blue box, because I didn't want to take it home and I didn't want to destroy it. And I never went back." She turned her cup round on its saucer. "I didn't know there was anything else on it. I chose that tape by chance. Out of thirty blank tapes, I picked the one he had used to practise."
"He must have erased it and thrown it on the pile," said Rui.
"Where nobody would ever look." Marta laughed, a short, painful sound. "Twenty-three years. And the proof was in my hand the whole time."

On the way home, Mari tried to imagine it: a sixteen-year-old girl alone in a tiny room, talking to the future in a foreign language because it felt safer than her own. She thought about the article in the newspaper. Anyone with a laptop can fake a voice. She understood now why the lawyers wanted every copy handed over. A digital file was just a digital file. It could be called a fake, a trick, an AI experiment by bored teenagers. But the cassette itself, the real one, with Marta's handwriting on the label and twenty-three years of dust in its case, was something else. Sandra could prove the age of the tape. An expert could prove that the ghost of Side B had been there since 2003.
The cassette was the only thing that could not be argued with.
She ran up the stairs to the flat. She went straight to her room and opened the drawer of her desk, where it had been kept since January, wrapped in one of Duarte's old football socks.
The sock was there. The cassette was not.

She searched the whole drawer, then the desk, then the floor, then her bag, with her heart beating in her throat. Duarte, when she asked him, signed that nobody had been in her room. Then he stopped, and thought, and signed something that made her sit down on the bed.
Leonor came round yesterday. She said she'd left her charger here. I let her in.
Mari's phone buzzed in her hand. One message, from Leonor.
Friday, 6 p.m. School auditorium. The exchange is going live. Bring everyone.

chapters.title: For Whoever Finds This
paragraphs: By a quarter to six on Friday, the auditorium was fuller than Mari had ever seen it.

The rows at the front were taken by the students from the media exchange, together with their parents and half the teachers in the school. A camera on a tripod pointed at the stage, where two chairs, a small table and two microphones had been set up in front of the old brown curtains. On a big screen at the back of the stage, three other rooms were waiting: a classroom in Cork full of students in green jumpers, a hall in Accra where someone was testing a microphone and laughing, and a library in Pune, where it was already late in the evening and a teacher was handing out cups of tea.

Mari stood at the side of the stage, by the steps, which was where Ms Doyle had asked her to stand. Duarte was in the second row. Two seats along from him sat Mr Salgado, in a jacket that was too big for him and a tie he had probably not worn for twenty years. Beside him, very straight, as if she were waiting for an exam result, sat Marta Quintela. Rui was next to his mother. He had not let go of her hand since they had come in.
Tobi was in charge of the sound. He gave Mari a thumbs-up from behind the mixing desk, which was the most nervous thumbs-up she had ever seen.
At six o'clock exactly, the lights went down, and Leonor walked onto the stage.
Behind her came her father.

A whisper went round the room, because almost everyone recognised him. Paulo Brás sat down in the second chair, adjusted his microphone like the professional he was, and smiled at the audience. It was his television smile, warm and easy. Only his hands gave him away. He kept them flat on his knees, as if they might otherwise do something he could not control.

Mari had agreed, earlier that week, to do something she had never done in public. Since Duarte would be in the audience, someone had to sign for him, and Ms Doyle had asked whether Mari would do it. So she stood under a small light at the edge of the stage, where the camera could see her, and as Leonor began to speak, Mari's hands began to move.

"Good evening, Cork, Accra and Pune, and good evening, Lisbon," said Leonor. Her voice was steady. "This is Second Take, the podcast of the Calçada, and tonight we're going to tell you a story about a radio station in our school, which closed twenty-three years ago, and a girl whose voice nobody wanted to hear."
She took something out of her pocket and put it on the table. A cassette in a cracked plastic case.
Then she played it.

Marta's voice filled the auditorium, through the old speakers that Mr Abílio had spent the afternoon reconnecting. If you are listening to this, then somebody has finally opened the box. In the second row, Marta closed her eyes. Rui put his arm round her shoulders. Up on the screen, in all three rooms on three continents, people had stopped moving.
After Marta's voice came Side B, cleaned and reversed. A boy laughing. Nobody will ever know it was me.
Leonor turned to the man beside her.
"Dad," she said, "is that your voice?"

The silence went on for so long that somebody in Cork coughed, and the sound came out of the speakers like a gunshot. Paulo Brás looked at his daughter. Then he looked at the second row, where a woman in a grey jacket and an old man in a borrowed tie were looking back at him. For a moment, Mari thought he was going to stand up and walk out. She thought he was going to say that it was all a fake, that anyone with a laptop could do it, exactly as the newspaper had said.
He leaned towards the microphone.

Afterwards, people would tell the story in different ways, and the newspapers would report it in a dozen versions, most of them wrong. But Mari, who had been signing every word of it with shaking hands, remembered it exactly.

He admitted that the voice was his. He said that he had been seventeen, angry and stupid, and that Mr Salgado had caught him cheating in a test, which he had deserved. He explained that he had recorded the bulletin as a joke, a revenge that was supposed to last one afternoon, and that he had never imagined it would end a man's career. He confessed that he had watched Marta take the blame and had said nothing, because saying something would have cost him too much. He said he had known for twenty-three years that he should tell the truth, and that he had been waiting for a moment when it would be easier, and that the moment had never come. Then he turned to the second row and apologised, first to Marta and then to Mr Salgado, without asking either of them to forgive him.
Nobody clapped. It was not that kind of moment.

Leonor, whose hands were also shaking, finished the episode. She thanked the schools in Cork, Accra and Pune. She explained what Rádio Eco had been, and why she thought that a radio station in a school mattered, and why a voice that is not believed is a voice that has been stolen. Her voice cracked once, on the word "believed", and then she went on.
Mari found her afterwards in the radio studio behind the stage, sitting on the floor under the shelves with her knees pulled up to her chin.
"You took the tape," said Mari, sitting down next to her.

"I'm sorry. I needed it." Leonor wiped her nose on her sleeve. "I told him on Wednesday. I said I would play it live, and that he could either be there and say something, or not be there and let other people say it for him. I wanted to give him one chance to do it himself. Although, honestly, I didn't think he would come."
"But he did."

"He did." Leonor laid her head on Mari's shoulder, the way she had done in the sandpit in Graça when they were six. "He's still my dad. That's the worst part. I'm so angry with him, and he's still my dad."

Things happened quickly after that, as they always do once a story has been told. The following week, the television channel announced that Paulo Brás was taking a break from the evening news. The newspaper published a correction, which was much shorter than the original article, on a page nobody read. The hearing against Rui was cancelled, although Dr Monteiro made him spend the last two weeks of term helping Mr Abílio clear the auditorium, which he did without complaining, mostly. She also wrote a letter to Henrique Salgado, which he read standing up in his shop and then put inside a copy of Great Expectations, where he said it would be safe.

On the last day of term, Marta came to the bookshop. Mari was there, by chance, returning a dictionary. She saw the old man look up, and the woman in the doorway, and she quietly found something very interesting to read on a shelf at the back.
"You were always a terrible liar," Mr Salgado said.
"I know," said Marta, and laughed, and then started crying, and he put the kettle on.

Tobi's mother's contract was extended for two more years. Tobi said it was a disaster, because he had only just learnt to say constipado in the right situations, and now he would have to learn the rest of the language as well. Then he asked Duarte to teach him the sign for friend, and got it right the first time.

On the very last afternoon, when the school was almost empty, Mari went back to the room behind the stage. She had a blank cassette in her pocket, bought from a man at the Feira da Ladra who could not believe his luck. She put it in the old player and pressed record.

"If you are listening to this," she said, in English, and then in Portuguese, and then she laughed, because the language she spoke best of all could not be recorded on a tape, "then somebody has finally opened the box. My name is Mariana Lobo, and I want you to know that someone listened."
She wrote on the label in blue ink: Para quem encontrar. M. Then she put it on shelf 3, behind the blue box, and turned off the light.

reading.title: The Room Behind the Stage
text: The new English teacher arrived ten minutes late, with wet hair, a bicycle helmet under one arm and a cardboard box of cassette tapes balanced on her hip. "I'm Fiona Doyle," she said. "I'm from Cork, which is in Ireland, which is not in England, so if anyone calls me English, I'll fail them. That's a joke. Mostly."

Mariana Lobo, who had chosen the seat by the window because it was the closest thing to an exit, laughed a second too late. She had spent the whole summer promising herself that secondary school would be different. She would speak in class. She would stop translating every sentence in her head three times before she said it out loud. So far, she had managed to sit down.

Ms Doyle explained the project for the term. The class was going to make "a map of voices", recording people who speak the languages that actually live in Lisbon. A new student, Tobi Adeyemi, who had arrived from London nineteen days earlier, asked whether English with a London accent counted. Mari realised she was doing what she always did with new people: guessing which of her languages she would need. Portuguese with her friends. English with films and books. And with her brother Duarte, who had been deaf since birth, Portuguese Sign Language, the language in which she was fastest, funniest and least afraid. Nobody at school had ever asked her about that one.

When Ms Doyle asked for volunteers to sort out the old student radio studio, Rádio Eco, Mari's best friend Leonor put her hand up for both of them. That afternoon, behind the stage of the auditorium, the caretaker unlocked a narrow door. "Nobody has been in here since I started working here," he said. "And I started in 2004."

The room was tiny. A mixing desk sat under a window that had been painted black, and the shelves were full of boxes of tapes. While the girls were working, Mari found a yellow sticky note in her English textbook, right next to the words find out. It had not been there at lunchtime. In block capitals, someone had written: SHELF 3. BEHIND THE BLUE BOX.

Behind the blue box there was a single cassette in a cracked case. The label said, in faded blue ink: Para quem encontrar. M. 14/03/2003. For whoever finds this. Mari pushed it into an old cassette player, and a girl's voice spoke in slow, careful English: "They are going to tell you that I did it, and I want you to know that I didn't. I know who did it. I just can't prove it yet. So I have left..." Then there was a heavy clunk, and nothing but hiss.

Behind them, the door creaked. Rui Câmara, a sixteen-year-old who was repeating the year, was standing in the doorway, staring at the cassette player. "You shouldn't be in here," he said. "Give me that tape."

My grandmother lives in a village near Viseu, and she uses expressions I never hear in Lisbon, so sometimes I have to ask her what she means. English is different. I mostly use it online, when I watch series or play games with people from other countries, and I feel a bit braver in English, maybe because nobody knows me there. Last summer I tried to speak French with a family at a campsite in the Algarve. It was a disaster, but they were patient, and in the end we communicated with gestures and a lot of laughter. reading.title: A Map of Voices
text: October arrived with the smell of roast chestnuts on every corner. For the language project, Mari, Leonor and Tobi spent a Saturday in Mouraria, one of the oldest and most multilingual neighbourhoods in Lisbon. Leonor had prepared eleven questions and printed them. "We should have finished by lunchtime," she said. They had not finished by four o'clock. Mouraria did not work like a list of questions.

In a narrow grocery shop that smelled of cardamom, Mr Rahman explained that he spoke Bengali at home, Portuguese with his customers, Hindi from the films he had watched as a boy in Dhaka and English with "everybody else in the world". "In my house we speak three languages at dinner," he said, "and we argue in all of them."

On a bench by the church, Dona Celeste, who had come from Cape Verde in 1979, laughed at Leonor's first question until she had to wipe her eyes. "Portuguese with a funny accent? No. Kriolu is not broken Portuguese. It's my language. It has its own grammar, its own songs." Leonor looked at her printed questions as if they had betrayed her. "That was a bit unfair of me," she admitted later. "It was disrespectful."

Tobi talked for twenty minutes with a delivery rider from Nepal who had learnt his English in Kathmandu. Afterwards he told the girls something that had clearly been on his mind for a long time. "In London, people used to correct my mum's English. In shops, at the doctor's. English is an official language in Nigeria. She's been speaking it her whole life. It's just not their English."

Mari's twelve-year-old brother Duarte, who is deaf, came with them. He signed comments to Mari so fast that Tobi stared. Mari explained that sign languages are not universal: British Sign Language and American Sign Language, for example, are completely different from each other. "So if I'd learnt sign language in London," said Tobi, "it wouldn't have helped me here at all?" "Not much."

It was Duarte who found the bookshop, Livraria Babel, so small that the sign was wider than the window. An old man with a white beard, Henrique Salgado, greeted Duarte in slow but correct sign language. He had once had a deaf student, he said, when he taught at the Calçada, a long time ago.

A week later, Mari went back alone with the mysterious cassette and played it in the shop. When the girl's voice said "I want you to know that I didn't", the old man's face went the colour of old paper. He stopped the tape, locked the door and stood looking out at the street. "Her name is Marta Quintela," he said at last. "And the thing they said she did, they did it to me."

fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 3 · Grammar: past tenses, perfect modals (criticism), word formation (nouns)

reading.title: Lunchtime News
text: Mr Salgado made tea before he told her the story. "In 2003, I had been teaching English at the Calçada for nineteen years," he said at last. "I was strict. Boring, probably. But I had never done anything wrong, and I thought that was enough."

"The student radio played music at lunchtime. There were speakers in every corridor and in the canteen. On the fourteenth of March, in the middle of the programme, there was a news bulletin. A fake one. A young man's voice said that a teacher, Professor Henrique Salgado, had been selling the answers to the national exams. It lasted forty seconds. By the time I had finished my soup, three hundred students had heard it."

"There was an inquiry. It took four months, and at the end of it they wrote a letter that said I was innocent. But by then a local newspaper had printed the story, parents had phoned the school, and people in the café on my street had stopped saying good morning. When you're accused of something on Monday, it's news. When you're cleared in July, nobody is listening." He left teaching the following year and opened the bookshop.

Marta Quintela had been the presenter that day. The bulletin was on a cassette in her pile of tapes, and she played it. She said she had never seen it before. Nobody believed her, and her parents moved her to another school before Easter. "I always thought she was telling the truth," said Mr Salgado. "She was a terrible liar."

When Mari told her friends, Leonor was unusually quiet. "My dad always says a story only needs to sound true for about five minutes," she said. "After that, people don't check. They just remember." Leonor's father, Paulo Brás, presented the evening news on national television.

In the school yearbook for 2002/03, they found a photo of the Rádio Eco team: eight teenagers around the mixing desk, and a list of first names. Ana. Marta. Pedro. Paulo. Sofia. Nuno. Joana. Rui. The girl in the middle had short dark hair and was laughing.

On Christmas Eve, Tobi and his mum had dinner with Mari's family. Tobi studied the boiled cod and cabbage as if it were a science experiment, and explained that in his house there would be jollof rice. Later he tried to say in Portuguese that he was ill and announced that he was "constipado". "In Portuguese it means you've got a cold," Mari laughed. "It's a false friend." "It's a terrible friend," said Tobi.

On the last day of term, Rui caught up with Mari at the school gate. "You played the tape to Salgado," he said. "He phoned my mother. First time in twenty-two years." In the light of the street lamp, Mari saw the same dark eyes as the laughing girl in the yearbook. "My name is Rui Quintela Câmara," he said. "Marta is my mum. And I'm the one who put that note in your book."

fichas.title: Side B
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 4 · Grammar: conditionals, have something done, phrasal verbs

reading.title: Side B
text: In January, Rui sat down opposite Mari in the library and explained why he had chosen her. He was not allowed in the auditorium because he had broken a window there the year before. "And I'd seen you," he said. "Reading books in English that weren't for school. Signing to your brother at the bus stop. You notice things." He had found out about the tape after he had heard his mother on the phone, saying: "If I had kept the tape, none of this would still be hurting."

The cassette had been played so many times that Mari was afraid it would snap, so Tobi suggested having it digitised. "My mum's company has a sound lab," he said. "If we had the tape copied properly, we could clean the sound up and actually look at it. Sound is just data. If you turn it into a picture, you can see things you'd never hear."

While an engineer called Sandra worked, they watched Tobi's mum on a video call through a glass wall, switching between English and Yoruba while a grandmother in Lagos waved at the camera. "My whole family runs on voice notes," said Tobi. "Seven, eight minutes long. Nobody in Nigeria wants to type if they can talk." Mari's grandmother, on the other hand, still phoned the landline every Sunday at eight. Duarte made video calls in sign language with his friends. And Rui's mother had an old phone with no internet. "She says she's had enough of things that stay on record forever," Rui said quietly.

On Sandra's screen, the recording became a spectrogram, a picture of sound. The clunk in Marta's message was not the end of the tape: something had hit the microphone, and then she had stopped recording. But Sandra had noticed something else. Under the hiss there was a faint, warbling sound, like a voice under water.

"It's the other side," she explained. "Somebody recorded silence over side B. But old machines never erased everything. There's a ghost of the original recording left, and some of it has leaked across. That's why it's backwards." When she reversed and cleaned it, a boy's voice came out of the speakers: "Lunchtime news... Henrique Salgado... selling the answers to the national exams..." Then, relaxed and laughing: "She never checks the tapes. Quintela just plays whatever's on the pile. Nobody will ever know it was me."
Rui walked out without a word. "If someone had found this in 2003," said Leonor slowly, "everything would have been different." Mari said nothing. She felt she had heard that voice before, somewhere.
That night, at a quarter to midnight, her phone buzzed. A new follower with no photo and no posts, called @radioeco2003, and a message: You found Side B. Be careful who you play it to.

writing.task: Write a blog post (120 to 180 words) comparing how different generations in your family communicate with technology (voice notes, calls, messages, video calls). Use at least two conditional sentences.
writing.model: In my family, every generation has its own way of keeping in touch. My grandparents, who live in Beja, still prefer the landline. If you don't answer on Sunday afternoon, my grandmother calls again and again until somebody picks up. My mum loves voice notes. She records them while she is cooking, and if she has something important to say, she sends five in a row. My dad is the opposite: he types short messages with no full stops, and he never uses emojis. My cousins and I mostly use video calls and group chats, and we send each other memes instead of long explanations. Sometimes I think my grandmother is right, though. fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 5 · Grammar: passive voice, mixed conditionals, collocations

reading.title: Taken Down
text: For a week after the message, nothing happened. Then, on the Thursday before Carnival, the account woke up. The first post appeared at twenty past ten, during break: a black square with white letters. IN 2003, A GIRL WAS BLAMED FOR A LIE. SHE SAID SHE DIDN'T DO IT. NOBODY LISTENED. Underneath there was a forty-second clip of Marta's voice.

By lunchtime it had been shared by half the school. By the end of the day, it had been viewed eleven thousand times. Everybody had a theory. The voice was an actress. The voice was AI. The whole thing was a marketing campaign for a series. Somebody found the old newspaper article and posted a photo of it. Mari watched it happen with a cold feeling in her stomach. It was like watching a fire you had accidentally started spread across a field.

On Friday she was called to the head teacher's office. "This has been brought to my attention by three parents, a journalist and the Ministry," said Dr Monteiro. "The posts have been reported, and I've had the account taken down twice this week. It keeps coming back." Mari's locker was searched, but nothing was found. At the door, the head said something that followed Mari all the way home: "If you had brought that tape to me in September, we wouldn't be in this situation now."
It was true, and that was the worst part. If she hadn't opened the box, she wouldn't be in this mess. Her whole life suddenly seemed to be made of sentences that started with if.

On Saturday, at the Carnival parade in Torres Vedras, Tobi was dressed as a cassette tape. "In London, my school locked our phones in pouches every morning," he said. "A rumour moves at the speed of whatever it's riding on. In 2003 it was a radio. Now it's this." He waved at the crowd, where a hundred people were filming the same float. "And you can't switch this off."

Leonor had been strange for days. Her father, a famous TV journalist, had told his colleagues to drop a story about the clip. "He never tells anyone to drop a story," she said. "He'd report on a cat stuck in a tree if it got viewers."

On Monday, at twenty past ten, everyone's phone buzzed along the corridor. A new clip had been posted. This time it was the boy's voice from side B: Nobody will ever know it was me. Mari's hands went cold. Side B had never been shared with anyone. It was kept in one place only, a folder that four people could open. It had been posted by one of them.

reading.title: Faces Without Sound
text: Mari found Rui behind the sports hall. She held out her phone with the clip on the screen. "Was it you?" He did not even try to deny it. "Yes. All of it." He had copied side B from Tobi's folder. "I didn't break into anything. He gave me the link."
"I was called into Monteiro's office," said Mari. "They searched my locker. She thinks I did it."

"I'm sorry. I didn't think they'd go after you." He stopped and started again. "Twenty-two years, Mari. Twenty-two years my mum has been the girl who did it. She didn't go to university. She works nights in a hotel and she doesn't have the internet because she's scared of her own name. If somebody had made a mess in 2003, my mum wouldn't be like this now."

Leonor arrived shouting. She called Rui a coward who was hiding behind a username, and she looked, Mari thought, much angrier than the situation explained. In the end, Mari asked Rui to take the clips down. "Give us time to find out who the boy is. If we know his name, we won't need the internet." Rui nodded, and the account disappeared while they watched.

Finding the boy was harder than they had imagined. A voice comparison app gave random answers. Then, in early March, Mr Abílio brought them three old video cassettes from the archive. One label said FESTA DA PRIMAVERA 14/03/2003, the day of the fake bulletin. They had the tape converted at a shop near Rossio, but damp had destroyed the sound. Only the images were left.

They watched it at Mari's flat, with her brother Duarte on the floor. Leonor had said she couldn't come. On the screen, the narrow door behind the stage opened. A tall boy came out, laughing, and slid a cassette into his pocket. Another boy was waiting. The tall one said something, looked back at the studio door and said something else. There was no sound, just two mouths moving in silence.

Duarte, who had been reading lips since before he could tie his shoelaces, played it three times. Then he signed to Mari, and she translated: "He says: 'Done. It's on her pile.' And then: 'Relax. She'll take the blame, not me.'"

As if he had heard them, the boy turned and grinned at the camera. Mari pressed pause. The face was younger and had too much gel in its hair, but she knew it. She had seen it on television a thousand times, reading the evening news. She had seen it at the head of a kitchen table in Graça. It was Paulo Brás. It was Leonor's father.

writing.task: "Anonymous accounts on social media do more harm than good." Write a short argumentative text (120 to 180 words), giving arguments for and against and your own conclusion. Refer to Rui's case if you wish.
writing.model: Anonymous accounts are everywhere online, and they are often used to insult or threaten people without any consequences. This is the strongest argument against them. When nobody knows who you are, it is easy to forget that there is a real person on the other side of the screen. Rui's account, for example, put Mari in a very difficult position, because she was blamed for posts she had not written. On the other hand, anonymity can protect people who have something important to say but are afraid to say it openly. Whistle-blowers, victims of bullying and people who live in countries without freedom of speech sometimes depend on it. If Marta had been able to speak anonymously in 2003, perhaps someone would have listened. In my opinion, anonymity itself is not the problem; the way it is used is. Platforms should act quickly against abuse, but they should not remove the right to stay anonymous completely.

fichas.title: What Friends Are For
fichas.focus: Reading: Chapter 7 · Grammar: reported speech, reporting verbs, relative clauses

reading.title: What Friends Are For
text: Duarte looked up at his sister and signed, small and fast: That's Leonor's dad. Mari signed back: Not a word. Not to anyone. Rui, who could not read sign language but could read faces, asked her if she knew the man. "I thought I did. I don't," she said. It was the first real lie she had told in months, and Rui did not believe a word of it.
She told Tobi the truth an hour later, on the phone. "My grandad used to say that a secret is a debt," Tobi said. "Somebody always pays for it. The question is just who."

During the Easter holidays, Mari visited Henrique Salgado. He was not surprised. "Paulo Brás. Of course. I failed him in his final English test. I caught him copying. He told me I would regret it." Then he gave her some advice. "The truth arrives late, but it does arrive. However, it isn't your truth to throw at your friend like a stone. If you do that, you'll lose her, whether you're right or not."

When school started again, Rui had been suspended. Dr Monteiro had told his mother that the account was a form of cyberbullying, and she had warned that he would be expelled if it happened again. Rui had refused to apologise, and he had also refused to say how he had got the clips.

Meanwhile, Leonor's podcast had been chosen for an online youth media exchange which Ms Doyle had organised with schools in Cork, Accra and Pune. Each school had to produce an episode on a story that mattered to young people in their community. The students in Accra were making an episode about music on social media, the ones in Pune were investigating how fake news travels through family group chats, and the class in Cork had chosen emigration. "And we're doing Rádio Eco," Leonor announced. "My dad says it's a terrible idea. Which means it's a great one."

That week, Ms Doyle held a debate in English class. The motion was: A good friend always tells the truth. Gonçalo argued that if everyone said what they really thought, nobody would have any friends. Tobi said that it depended on whose truth it was and who would get hurt. Leonor spoke last. "If someone you love has done something wrong, you have to know. I would rather be hurt than be lied to." She was not looking at Mari, but Mari felt the words land in her chest like something heavy and cold.

On Friday, Leonor's laptop died, so she came round to borrow Mari's. When Mari came back from the kitchen with tea, the room was very quiet. On the screen, frozen in the middle of a grin, was the boy with too much gel in his hair. Leonor did not turn round. "How long have you known?"

writing.task: "A good friend always tells the truth." Write your contribution to Ms Doyle's debate (120 to 180 words). State your opinion clearly, give reasons and an example, and use at least one reported sentence (e.g. "My grandmother once told me that...").
writing.model: I partly agree with the motion. In most situations, a good friend should tell the truth, even when it is uncomfortable. If my friend has spinach in her teeth before a presentation, I will tell her, because a small moment of embarrassment is better than a big one. Friendships that are based on lies usually break in the end, and the person who discovers the lie feels twice as hurt. However, I don't think the truth should be told in any way, at any moment. My grandmother once told me that the truth is like medicine: the right dose helps, but too much at the wrong time can make you ill. Sometimes a friend needs time, or needs to hear something from the right person. Telling the truth is not the same as throwing it at someone. So, in my opinion, a good friend never lies about important things, but thinks carefully about how and when to speak.

reading.title: Off the Record
text: For two weeks, Leonor did not speak to Mari. Then, at ten past two on a Thursday morning, Mari's phone lit up with an eleven-minute voice note. Leonor said that she had shown her father the frame from the video. At first he had laughed. Then he had told her that the video proved nothing, that it was a silent film of a teenager coming out of a room. He had warned her that if the story came out, it would destroy the family, and he had begged her to cancel the episode.

"And here's the thing, Mari," said Leonor's voice in the dark. "He never said he didn't do it. Not once. He said I couldn't prove it. That's not the same, is it?" Then, after a long pause: "I'm still angry with you. But I think I understand why you didn't tell me."

At the beginning of May, a national newspaper published a short article about "a cyberbullying case at a Lisbon secondary school". It quoted a source who claimed that the recordings could easily have been manipulated, "especially now, when anyone with a laptop can fake a voice". Two days later, the head received a letter from a law firm whose client wanted all copies of the recordings to be handed over and destroyed.

It was Rui who arranged a meeting with his mother. They met at seven o'clock on a Saturday morning in a café in Alfama, at the end of Marta's night shift. She told them that she had suspected Paulo from the start, because he was the boy who had threatened Mr Salgado. She said she had gone to the head the day after the bulletin, but he had told her not to make accusations she could not support. "Paulo was everyone's favourite. I was the girl from the flats behind the market. You can guess whose word was worth more."

The week before she left the school, Marta had gone back to the studio and picked up a blank tape from the pile on the shelf to record a message for the future. "Then the door opened, and it was him." She had hit the microphone, stopped the tape and hidden it behind the blue box. "I didn't know there was anything else on it. Out of thirty blank tapes, I picked the one he had used to practise."

On the way home, Mari understood why the lawyers wanted every copy. A digital file could be called a fake. The original cassette, however, with Marta's handwriting and twenty-three years of dust, was the only thing that could not be argued with.

She ran up to her room and opened the drawer where she had kept it since January. The cassette was gone. Duarte signed that Leonor had come round the day before to look for a charger. Then Mari's phone buzzed. Friday, 6 p.m. School auditorium. The exchange is going live. Bring everyone.

reading.title: For Whoever Finds This
text: By six o'clock on Friday, the auditorium was full. On a big screen, three other rooms were waiting: a classroom in Cork, a hall in Accra and a library in Pune. In the second row sat Mr Salgado, in a tie he had probably not worn for twenty years, and beside him Marta Quintela, with Rui holding her hand. Since Duarte was in the audience, Mari stood at the edge of the stage to translate everything into sign language, something she had never done in public.

Leonor walked onto the stage, and behind her came her father. Paulo Brás sat down and smiled his television smile. Only his hands gave him away: he kept them flat on his knees. "This is Second Take," said Leonor, "and tonight we're going to tell you about a radio station in our school, which closed twenty-three years ago, and a girl whose voice nobody wanted to hear." She put a cassette on the table and played it. Marta's voice filled the room, then the boy's voice from side B. Nobody will ever know it was me.
"Dad," said Leonor, "is that your voice?"

The silence went on so long that somebody in Cork coughed. Then Paulo Brás leaned towards the microphone. He admitted that the voice was his. He said that he had been seventeen, angry and stupid, and that Mr Salgado had caught him cheating, which he had deserved. He explained that the bulletin was supposed to be a revenge that lasted one afternoon. He confessed that he had watched Marta take the blame and said nothing. Finally, he apologised to Marta and to Mr Salgado, without asking either of them to forgive him. Nobody clapped. It was not that kind of moment.

Later, Mari found Leonor sitting on the floor of the radio studio. Leonor explained that she had taken the tape because she wanted to give her father one chance to tell the truth himself. "Although, honestly, I didn't think he would come. He's still my dad. That's the worst part."

The following week, the TV channel announced that Paulo Brás was taking a break from the news. The newspaper published a correction, much shorter than the original article. The case against Rui was cancelled, although he had to help the caretaker for the last two weeks of term. Tobi's mother's contract was extended, so he would stay in Lisbon.

On the last afternoon, Mari went back to the room behind the stage with a blank cassette. "If you are listening to this," she said, in English and then in Portuguese, laughing, because the language she spoke best could not be recorded on a tape, "then somebody has finally opened the box. My name is Mariana Lobo, and I want you to know that someone listened." She wrote on the label: Para quem encontrar. M. Then she put it on shelf 3, behind the blue box.

What I value most is my group of friends, because they accept me even when I'm in a bad mood. I also value honesty, although I know it is not always easy. sebenta.title: Verb tenses: present and past
sebenta.html:
Present Simple

FormUseExamples
I/you/we/they work
he/she/it works
neg.: don't / doesn't + verb
quest.: Do / Does + subject + verb?		 • habits and routines
• permanent situations, facts
• timetables and schedules
• with adverbs of frequency		 She works in a bank.
Water boils at 100 °C.
The train leaves at 9.15.
I always get up early.

Adverbs of frequency: always · usually · often · sometimes · rarely / seldom · hardly ever · never. They go before the main verb but after be: He never complains. / He is never late. Spelling of the 3rd person: watches, goes, studies, plays.

Present Continuous

FormUseExamples
am / is / are + verb-ing • actions happening now
• temporary situations
• changing situations
• fixed future arrangements
• annoying habits (+ always)		 She's talking on the phone.
I'm staying with a friend this week.
Prices are rising.
We're meeting at 8 tomorrow.
He's always losing his keys!
Stative verbs are not normally used in continuous tenses: know, believe, understand, want, need, like, love, hate, prefer, belong, own, seem, mean. I want a coffee (not I'm wanting). Some change meaning: I think it's good (opinion) / I'm thinking about it (process); I have a car (own) / I'm having lunch (activity).

Past Simple

FormUseExamples
regular: verb + -ed
irregular: 2nd column (p. 14)
neg.: didn't + verb
quest.: Did + subject + verb?		 • finished actions at a definite time in the past
• a sequence of past events
• past habits and states		 We visited Rome last year.
She opened the door and went in.
I lived in Porto as a child.

Time markers: yesterday · last week/year · two days ago · in 2015 · when I was a child.

Past Continuous

FormUseExamples
was / were + verb-ing • action in progress at a past moment
• background to a shorter action (past simple)
• two parallel actions		 At 8 pm I was having dinner.
I was walking home when it started to rain.
While I was cooking, he was reading.
Past Simple vs Past Continuous: when + past simple interrupts; while / as + past continuous gives the background. The phone rang while I was sleeping.

sebenta.title: Verb tenses: perfect tenses
sebenta.html:
Present Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
have / has + past participle (3rd column, p. 14) • unfinished past (started in the past, continues now) → for / since
• life experience → ever, never, before
• recent news / results evident now → just, already, yet
• tasks done / not done up to now		 I've lived here for ten years / since 2016.
Have you ever been to London?
She has just arrived. · I've lost my keys!
I've already finished; he hasn't started yet.

Markers: for · since · ever · never · just · already · yet · so far · recently · lately · this week · today · how long…?

Present Perfect Continuous

FormUseExamples
have / has been + verb-ing • unfinished activity, emphasis on duration
• repeated actions up to now
• activity just stopped, results evident now		 I've been studying for three hours.
She's been calling you all morning.
You're red – have you been running?
Simple vs Continuous: simple = result / how many (I've written three emails); continuous = activity / how long (I've been writing emails all day). Stative verbs → simple only (I've known him for years).
Past Simple vs Present Perfect: finished time (yesterday, in 2010, ago) → past simple; time up to now (today, this year, ever, since) → present perfect. I saw him yesterday. / I have seen him today. Note: been = went and came back; gone = not back yet.

Past Perfect Simple

FormUseExamples
had + past participle • an action completed before another past action or moment ("the past of the past")
• with by the time, after, before, when, already, never…before
• in reported speech and 3rd conditional		 When I arrived, the film had already started.
She had never flown before that day.
By 2020 they had moved twice.

Past Perfect Continuous

FormUseExamples
had been + verb-ing • activity in progress up to a past moment, emphasis on duration
• cause of a past situation		 He had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.
Her eyes were red – she had been crying.

Tenses together: I have known Ana since we were at school. · It has been raining since I got up. · By the time we got there, the shop had closed.

sebenta.html:
FormUseExamples

Going to

• predictions based on evidence		We're going to buy a flat.
Look at those clouds – it's going to rain.
Will
will + verb		• spontaneous decisions, offers, promises, requests
• predictions based on opinion (I think, probably)
• facts about the future		I'll help you with that.

Future Perfect

Will vs going to: decision made now → will ("We've run out of milk." "I'll get some."); decision made before → going to (I'm going to get some milk – it's on my list.). After when, as soon as, until, before, after, if use the present, not will: I'll call you when I arrive.

Spelling of -ing and -ed

  • Final -e is dropped: make → making, live → lived.
  • One vowel + one consonant (stressed syllable): the consonant doubles: stop → stopping, plan → planned, begin → beginning.
  • Consonant + -y: -y → -ied in the past (study → studied), but -ing keeps the y (studying).
  • -ie → -ying: lie → lying, die → dying.

Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) are followed by the bare infinitive, have no -s in the 3rd person and form negatives and questions without do: She must go. · Can he swim? · You needn't worry. Semi-modals: have to, need to, be able to, ought to, be allowed to, had better.

sebenta.title: Modal verbs (2): perfect modals
sebenta.html:
Form: modal + have + past participle (must have done, should have gone, can't have been). Perfect modals look back at the past from the present: we deduce what happened, or we comment on what someone did or didn't do. Have is pronounced /əv/ – never write should of.

Possible (we don't know)may / might / could have + past part.She may have missed the train.
He might not have seen you.
Sure it did NOT happencan't / couldn't have + past part.He can't have finished already – it's a 3-hour exam!
You couldn't have met her; she was abroad.
The opposite of must have (certainty) is can't have, not mustn't have. Could have = possible; couldn't have = impossible.

Past ability not usedcould have + p.p.I could have gone to university, but I started working.
Expectation that didn't happenshould have + p.p. (= was expected)The bus should have arrived by now.
Unnecessary action that was doneneedn't have + p.p.You needn't have brought food – there's plenty. (you did, but it wasn't necessary)

sebenta.html:

  • Verbs with prepositions keep them: The children were looked after by their aunt. · The plan was laughed at.

Defining relative clauses

Give essential information to identify the noun. No commas. That can replace who / which. The pronoun can be omitted when it is the object of the clause: The film (which) we saw was great. · The woman (who) you met is my aunt. But not when it is the subject: The woman who called is my aunt.

Add extra information about a noun already identified; between commas. That is not used and the pronoun cannot be omitted. My brother, who lives in Faro, is a doctor. · Sintra, which is near Lisbon, is beautiful. Which can refer to a whole clause: He arrived late, which annoyed everyone.
